Lessons: Grade 8 US History

Ten lessons that teach Grade 8 US History with maps, arranged by topic in the order most courses teach them. Each one pairs a map with an inquiry, a Word student sheet in English and Spanish, and a separate teacher page with the answers.

10 lessons · US History · no account or login needed

Road to revolution and the Revolution

  • 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question

    Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.

Confederation and the Constitution

  • Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: The early republic

    Map the public places in your own community where people use the rights in the Bill of Rights and carry out their responsibilities as citizens, and find who represents your district in Congress.

  • We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: The early republic

    See how House seats were shared out after the 1790 census, how the three-fifths clause changed the count, and how close each state's vote to ratify was.

The early republic

  • Political Parties and Federal Power, 1796–1819

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question

    Compare how each state's electors voted in 1796 and 1800, see which states changed sides, and find two Supreme Court cases that shaped the new government. The elections of 1796 and 1800 show the first party divide; two Supreme Court cases, in 1803 and 1819, show how the new federal government's power was tested.

  • The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

    Compare the Louisiana Purchase with the United States of 1803, see why the Mississippi River and New Orleans mattered, and follow Lewis and Clark's route across rivers and biomes to the Pacific.

  • The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

    Find where the War of 1812 was fought, see what Spain gave up in 1819, and compare Latin America's new nations with the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.

Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

  • Roads, Trails, and Rails West

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration

    Follow the trails settlers took west in the 1800s, see whose lands they crossed, and find out how railroads replaced the wagon trails.

Reform and the road to war

  • US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration

    Compare free and slave states in 1850, follow the routes of the internal slave trade south, and trace the Underground Railroad north to freedom.

The Civil War

  • Civil War Battlefields

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question · also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration

    See how the United States was divided by 1863, compare the railroads of the North and the South, and find where the war's battles were fought.

  • The Battle of Vicksburg

    Grade 8 · 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question

    Follow Grant's 1863 march to Vicksburg along the Mississippi River, and see why taking the city split the Confederacy in two.

In every lesson

  • A map that opens straight from the page, with each layer’s source listed. No account or login is needed.
  • An inquiry with a compelling question and questions you can pick from, each answered from the map.
  • A Word student sheet in English and Spanish that you can edit, print or open in Google Docs.
  • A separate answer page, and a Word file, with where to find each answer on the map and what to accept.
  • Links to how-to videos, and a prompt for your own AI tool.

Lessons

How these lessons work

What every lesson includes, how to prepare, and ways to run one.

What every lesson includes

  • Each lesson is one map and a set of questions that students answer by using the map: opening bookmarks, clicking pop-ups, reading the legend, turning layers on and off and measuring. The questions can't be answered from a textbook alone.
  • Students need no account or login. Open map opens the map straight from the lesson page; the Share to Google Classroom button shares the map link with a class.
  • The Word student sheet (English and Spanish) is two pages: a big question, some background, help reading the map, the questions with space to write, and a closing reflection. Print it or share it digitally; it opens in Word and Google Docs.
  • Each lesson page lists the questions with the exact steps for the front of the class, marks one question as the one to use if you only have 15 minutes, and gives ideas for support and stretch.
  • Where to find each answer on the map, and what to accept, are on a separate answer page and in the Word teacher notes, so the lesson page can be shared with students.
  • Sketches on the map are not saved between sessions. Students who sketch should finish in one session or take a screenshot.
  • Each lesson page has a prompt to paste into an AI tool, which lists the map's layers so the tool doesn't invent any.

Ways to run a lesson

  • Front-of-class demonstration
  • 1:1 devices
  • Computer lab
  • Homework or flipped classroom

Materials

The lesson includes the map, a two-page Word student sheet in English and Spanish, and these teacher notes. Print the sheet, or download it and upload it to Google Drive to edit it in Google Docs (it also opens in Word). The Google Classroom button shares the map, not the sheet; to assign the sheet, attach your Drive copy in Classroom with Make a copy for each student, or paste the map link and attach the sheet yourself. No account or login is needed. Sketches on the map are not saved between sessions.

Preparing

  • Open the map and click through the bookmarks and pop-ups. Check the legend at the zoom levels the questions use; it changes as you zoom and as layers are turned on and off.
  • Decide whether students work alone, in pairs or as a whole class, and whether they use the printed sheet or a digital copy.
  • Encourage students to look for patterns and make observations, not just to find the right answers.
  • Layers the questions don't use are there for further study.

Assessing the answer to the big question

Every lesson ends with students answering the compelling question with evidence from the map. This rubric is one way to assess that answer; each lesson's answer page adds a line on what counts as map evidence for that map, and a model answer. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

Help

Short how-to videos for every map tool are on the MapMaker Educator Support Hub (opens in a new tab). Each lesson page has a Report a problem button that tells us which lesson you mean.

Inquiry

Compelling question

Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

Pick the questions that suit your class: each one is answered from the map and says about how long it takes. The one marked If you only do one gets to the big question on its own in about 15 minutes. Under each question, From the front gives the exact clicks for teaching it on a projector. Answers and what to accept are linked under Teacher notes.

  1. Where did the war begin? About 10 minutes

    Open the Massachusetts bookmark and click the Lexington and Concord diamond, then the Boston diamond. Read the dates in each pop-up, and the winner from the diamond's color and the legend. Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

    From the front

    1. Open the Massachusetts bookmark.
    2. Click the diamond at Lexington and Concord and read the date line.
    3. Open the legend and find which colour means an American victory.
    4. Ask: who won, and how do you know from the map?
    5. Click the Boston diamond and read its two dates.
    6. Ask: how long did the siege of Boston last?
    7. Use Measure for the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776? If you only do one About 15 minutes

    Zoom out until all 21 diamonds show, from Quebec to South Carolina. Click each one, read its dates, and sort the battles into two lists by year. Use the legend for the winner. Which colonies saw fighting each year, and what changed?

    From the front

    1. Zoom out until all 21 diamonds show, from Quebec to South Carolina.
    2. Click the Bunker Hill diamond and read the date line.
    3. Click the Brooklyn diamond and read the date line.
    4. Open the legend and check the colour of each of those two diamonds.
    5. Ask: which colonies had battles in 1775, and which in 1776?
    6. Ask: where did the fighting move to, and who was winning there?

    Tools: Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  3. Why New York? About 15 minutes

    Turn on Key Port Cities (it sits inside the Revolutionary War Battlefields group). Students use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port, name the major ports between Boston and Charleston (the layer has no pop-ups, so the battle diamonds and the coastline help), measure New York to Philadelphia and New York to Boston, and say what a navy based at New York could reach.

    From the front

    1. In Map layers, open Revolutionary War Battlefields and turn on Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781.
    2. Open the legend and show the larger symbol for a Major Port City and the smaller one for a Port.
    3. Ask: Boston and Charleston are major ports; which other major ports lie between them?
    4. Use Measure from New York to Philadelphia.
    5. Use Measure from New York to Boston.
    6. Ask: what could a navy based at New York reach?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  4. How did 1776 end? About 12 minutes

    Zoom in near New York City until the numbered turning points show, and follow circles 4 and 5. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton, and read the dates and the winner from the legend. Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton.

    From the front

    1. Zoom in on New York City until the numbered Turning Points circles appear.
    2. Click circle 4 and read the Battle details text.
    3. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington and Fort Lee and read their dates.
    4. Click circle 5, then the Trenton diamond, and read its date.
    5. Open the legend and check the colour of each diamond.
    6. Use Measure for the distance from New York City to Trenton.
    7. Ask: how did 1776 end for Washington's army?

    Tools: Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a route drawn with Sketch (not saved, so finish in one session or take a screenshot), or a short talk using the bookmark and the layers.

1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

Open the map: 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Before you start

British soldiers marched out of Boston to seize weapons that colonists had stored at Concord. The fighting that followed started the American Revolution. For the next two years, the British army and navy and the new Continental Army, led by George Washington, fought over the colonies' cities, rivers and harbors.

Reading the map

Diamonds mark battles. A battle's pop-up gives its name, dates and story, but not the winner in words: the diamond's color shows the winner, so use the legend. Each diamond is placed at the battle's usual location, but the fighting covered a wider area: gray shaded areas show the battlefield, and areas with diagonal stripes show the core, where the fighting was heaviest. Zoom in to see white numbered circles: five turning points, numbered in the order they happened. The Key Port Cities layer has no pop-ups: the legend tells a major port from a smaller one.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Where did the war begin?

    On the map:

    1. Open the Massachusetts bookmark.
    2. Click the diamond at Lexington and Concord and read its dates.
    3. Open the legend and check which color shows who won.
    4. Click the Boston diamond and read its dates.
    5. Use Measure for the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

    Answer: When was Lexington and Concord fought, and who won? How long did the siege of Boston last? Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord: miles

  2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?

    On the map:

    1. Zoom out until you can see every diamond, from Quebec to South Carolina.
    2. Click the diamonds and read each one's date line to see its year.
    3. Click the colony under each group of diamonds to read its name, and use the legend to see who won.

    Answer: Which colonies had battles in 1775? Which in 1776? What changed?

  3. Why New York?

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (inside Revolutionary War Battlefields).
    2. Use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port.
    3. Find the major ports between Boston and Charleston.
    4. The layer has no pop-ups, so use the coastline and the battle diamonds nearby to name them.
    5. Use Measure from New York to Philadelphia and from New York to Boston.

    Answer: Boston and Charleston are major ports: which other major ports lie between them? Looking at the map, what could a navy based at New York reach? New York to Philadelphia: miles. New York to Boston: miles

  4. How did 1776 end?

    On the map:

    1. Zoom in on New York City until the numbered circles appear.
    2. Follow circles 4 and 5.
    3. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton.
    4. Read each one's dates, and use the legend to see who won.
    5. Use Measure for the distance from New York City to Trenton.

    Answer: When was each battle fought, and who won? Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton: miles

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two places on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about 1775–1776 that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Subjects: US History, Geography, Social Studies. Grade: 8. Time: 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.

Learning objectives

Students will:

  • Locate the 21 battles of 1775–1776 on the map and sort them by year, using the pop-up dates and the legend for the winner.
  • Measure straight-line distances between Boston, Concord, New York, Philadelphia and Trenton with the Measure tool.
  • Identify the major ports between Boston and Charleston from the Key Port Cities layer and the coastline, and explain what a navy based at New York could reach.
  • Trace the end of 1776 through the numbered Turning Points and the Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton pop-ups.
  • Use evidence from at least two places on the map to explain why the fighting moved from Boston to New York and across New Jersey.

Map skills

  • Using bookmarks to find places
  • Reading pop-ups
  • Using a map legend
  • Measuring distances on a map
  • Navigating a map
  • Turning map layers on and off
  • Sketching on a map

Ways to run this lesson

  • Front-of-class demonstration
  • 1:1 devices
  • Computer lab
  • Homework or flipped classroom

Before class

About this map: Every layer is on when the map opens except Key Port Cities, which students turn on for question 3. The Massachusetts bookmark takes students to the first battles.

Materials, ways to prepare and how every lesson works are on How these lessons work.

Discussion questions

  1. Looking at where the 1775 battles cluster and where the 1776 battles cluster, what does the map suggest about each side's plan for the war?
  2. The Key Port Cities layer has no pop-ups, so you had to work out the ports from the coastline and the battle diamonds. What other clues on the map helped, and what was missing?
  3. Nearly every 1776 battle around New York was a British victory, yet the year ends with Trenton. Using the distances you measured, why might that one small battle have mattered so much?

Support and stretch

  • Support: Do question 1 together from the front and write the two diamond colours and what each means on the board before students start question 2.
  • Stretch: Find the 1763 Proclamation Line and ask whether any of the 21 battles were fought west of it, and what that says about where the war was being fought.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The early war was fought in Massachusetts.” By the end of 1776 the map shows battles in seven colonies and in Quebec.
  • “The winner is the side that lost fewer soldiers.” Bunker Hill is shown as a British victory, yet its pop-up says the British had twice as many casualties as the Patriots.
  • “The Americans lost every battle in 1776.” The map shows American wins in the South that year, such as Moores Creek Bridge and Sullivan's Island, as well as Trenton.

Key words

  • siege
  • militia
  • Continental Army
  • Loyalist
  • harbor
  • campaign
  • retreat

Where to find each answer on the map and what to accept are kept off this page, so it can be shared with students: answer notes (web page) or Download Word (teacher notes). The answer page also has a rubric for the answer to the compelling question and a model answer.

About this map

This map follows the first two years of the American Revolution, 1775 and 1776. It shows 21 battles from those years and the land their battlefields covered, against the colony borders of 1763 and the 1763 Proclamation Line. Five numbered turning points, which appear when you zoom in, mark the order of events from Lexington and Concord to Trenton. A layer of port cities, off when the map opens, adds the ports that supplied armies and moved troops.

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
Revolutionary War BattlesWhat it shows: 21 battles from April 1775 to December 1776. Each pop-up gives the battle's name and dates, a picture and a short account. The winner is shown only by the diamond's color, as listed in the legend (American Victory or British Victory); the pop-up does not state it in words.Source: American Battlefield Trust
Revolutionary War BattlefieldsWhat it shows: Battlefield boundaries (gray) and the core areas where the fighting was heaviest (diagonal stripes). No pop-ups.Source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program
Turning PointsWhat it shows: Five white circles numbered 1 to 5, from Lexington and Concord to Trenton, that appear when you zoom in. Each pop-up gives the event's name, year, a short account (the Battle_details field) and the victor.Source: Chris Bunin and Peter Trentacoste (2026), from National Park Service, US Army Center of Military History and Library of Congress sources
Thirteen British ColoniesWhat it shows: Colony areas and borders in 1763. The pop-up gives the colony's name.Source: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988)
1763 Proclamation LineWhat it shows: The line west of which King George III barred colonial settlement and land purchases, reserving the land beyond it for American Indian nationsSource: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988); the reservation is in the Proclamation's text (Avalon Project, Yale Law School (opens in a new tab))
Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Ports that supplied armies and moved troops, from New England to the Caribbean and Britain. The legend separates a Major Port City (larger symbol) from a smaller Port. The layer has no pop-ups and no labels.Source: Jay Feyerabend, master's thesis (opens in a new tab), James Madison University (2021)

Name Date

Big question: How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?

Open the map: Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Before you start

In the 1800s, hundreds of thousands of people from the eastern United States went west in wagons, looking for farmland, gold or a place to practice their religion freely. A journey along one of the trails could take months. Later in the century, railroads were built across the West.

Reading the map

Each trail is a dotted line in its own color; the legend names them, and clicking a trail opens its pop-up. City and state names are part of the basemap. Railroads and Indigenous Territories are off when the map opens: turn them on in Map layers. Thick colored lines are the transcontinental railroads, named in the legend, and thin gray lines are other railroads; only the thin gray lines have pop-ups. Each Indigenous nation's territory is shaded in its own color, and its name appears when you zoom in. The territories are approximate and aren't listed in the legend.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Where did the trails begin?

    On the map:

    1. Open the legend to see which color is which trail.
    2. Click three of the dotted trail lines.
    3. Read in each pop-up where the trail started and ended.

    Answer: Where did each trail start and end? In which state do most of the trails start?

  2. How far, and how many?

    On the map:

    1. Find the Oregon Trail's color in the legend.
    2. Click the Oregon Trail and read its length and how many people traveled it.
    3. Find Independence, Missouri, on the basemap, next to Kansas City.
    4. Use Measure for a straight line from Independence to Portland, Oregon.

    Answer: How long was the Oregon Trail, and how many people traveled it? Why is the trail longer than a straight line? Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon: miles

  3. Whose land?

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on Indigenous Territories.
    2. Zoom in until the nations' names appear.
    3. Follow one trail from one end to the other.
    4. Find two nations whose land it crossed.

    Answer: Which two nations' land did the trail cross? Was the land the trail crossed empty? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?

  4. From trails to rails

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on Railroads.
    2. Use the legend to find the Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and (Central Pacific) lines.
    3. Click a thin gray railroad line and read when it was in operation by.

    Answer: Which trails do the Transcontinental Railroad lines follow most closely? By when was the gray railroad line in operation?

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about the journey west that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: How did slavery divide the United States by 1850?

Open the map: US Slavery and Slave Trade, 1850

Before you start

By 1850, the Northern states had ended slavery or passed laws to end it, but in the South slavery was legal and growing. More than 3 million people were enslaved in the United States. Each time a new state joined the Union, Congress argued over whether slavery would be allowed there.

Reading the map

States and territories are shaded brown if they were free and green if they allowed slavery; the paler shades mean free, or slave, because of a compromise. Open the legend to see the four groups. Click a state to read its name and year in the pop-up. A gray dashed line marks the Missouri Compromise Line; click it for its pop-up. Solid black lines are internal routes of the slave trade. They have no arrows. Dashed and dotted lines in the same layer show sea routes and the voyages of two ships, the Amistad and the Creole. Orange lines are approximate Underground Railroad routes. Zoom in to see the towns along them: orange dots in the United States, black dots in Canada.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Free states and slave states

    On the map:

    1. Open the legend and find the four groups for US States and Territories 1850.
    2. Click a state in each group to read its name.
    3. Click two states to read what year each became free or slave.

    Answer: Which groups are free and which allow slavery? Where is the line between free and slave states in the East?

  2. The Missouri Compromise

    On the map:

    1. Find the Missouri Compromise Line (the gray dashed line).
    2. Click it and read its pop-up.
    3. Find the slave state that lies mostly north of the line.

    Answer: What year was the Missouri Compromise enacted? Slavery was banned north of the line in the Louisiana Territory: which slave state lies mostly north of it, and why does that matter?

  3. The internal slave trade

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn off Underground Railroad Approximate Routes so the solid black lines of Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade stand out.
    2. Click the states where the lines begin and read their names.
    3. Click the states where the lines come together and read their names.
    4. Find where the lines reach the coast.

    Answer: Where do the lines reach the coast? The lines have no arrows: from the pattern and what you have learned, which way were enslaved people forced to move?

  4. Routes to freedom

    On the map:

    1. Open the Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark.
    2. Follow the orange Underground Railroad routes north from the Ohio River.
    3. Zoom in to read the names of the towns along them.

    Answer: Where do the routes lead? Why do you think many keep going past the free states?

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about slavery in 1850 that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Discussion questions

  1. The slave-trade routes have no arrows, yet you worked out which way enslaved people were forced to move. What on the map told you, and what did you have to bring from outside the map?
  2. Many Underground Railroad routes keep going past Ohio, Indiana and Illinois to Canada. What does that tell you about what 'free state' meant in 1850?
  3. These layers were traced from a 1920 atlas. What might a map drawn today show differently, and why does that matter when we use old maps as evidence?

  • “Every Northern state banned slavery at the same time.” The pop-ups give a different year for each free state.

Inquiry

Compelling question

How did the geography of a divided nation shape the Civil War, as the map shows the country in 1863?

Pick the questions that suit your class: each one is answered from the map and says about how long it takes. The one marked If you only do one gets to the big question on its own in about 15 minutes. Under each question, From the front gives the exact clicks for teaching it on a projector. Answers and what to accept are linked under Teacher notes.

  1. A nation divided About 15 minutes

    Use the legend for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) to sort the states: which seceded before Fort Sumter, which after, and which slave states stayed in the Union? Then spot the state on this 1863 layer that did not exist in 1861 (West Virginia), as the way in to how the map's date matters.

    From the front

    1. Open the legend and show the five groups for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863).
    2. Point to South Carolina and match its shade to its legend group.
    3. Point to Virginia and match its shade.
    4. Point to Kentucky and match its shade.
    5. Ask: which states left before Fort Sumter, which after, and which slave states stayed in the Union?
    6. Ask: the layer shows 1863; which state on it did not exist in 1861?

    Tools: Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  2. The border states About 8 minutes

    Zoom to Washington, D.C. Which two states border it? Using the legend shades of those two states, what would have happened to the capital if Maryland had left the Union?

    From the front

    1. Zoom in to Washington, D.C., between Maryland and Virginia.
    2. Point to the white dashed Boundary between Union and Confederacy running past the capital.
    3. Open the legend and check Maryland's shade, then Virginia's.
    4. Ask: which two states border the capital, and which side was each on?
    5. Ask: what would have happened to Washington if Maryland had left the Union?

    Tools: Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  3. Railroads, North and South About 10 minutes

    Compare the Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static) layer (thin dark gray lines) north and south of the Boundary between Union and Confederacy (a white dashed line). Turning the States layer off in Map layers makes the lines easier to see. Which side had more railroads, and why would that matter in a war?

    From the front

    1. In Map layers, turn off U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863).
    2. Point to the thin dark gray lines of Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static).
    3. Follow the white dashed Boundary between Union and Confederacy from the Atlantic to the Mississippi.
    4. Ask: which side has more railroad lines?
    5. Ask: why would railroads matter in a war?
    6. Turn U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) back on.

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

    Zoom to Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania, and click the tan battlefield areas for names, sizes and state. Where were most battles fought, and which were fought in Union states (check the state's shade in the legend)?

    From the front

    1. Zoom to Virginia and point to the tan battlefield areas between Washington and Richmond.
    2. Click one tan area and read the battle's name, acres and state.
    3. Zoom to Maryland and Pennsylvania and click the tan area at Gettysburg.
    4. Open the legend and check Pennsylvania's shade.

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: How did the geography of a divided nation shape the Civil War, as the map shows the country in 1863?

Open the map: Civil War Battlefields

Before you start

In November 1860, Abraham Lincoln was elected president. He opposed the spread of slavery into the western territories, and Southern slave states began to leave the Union to form the Confederate States of America. In April 1861, Confederate forces attacked Fort Sumter, a Union fort in South Carolina, and the Civil War began.

Reading the map

States are shaded by side in 1863: shades of blue for the Union and shades of brown for the Confederacy; open the legend to see which shade means which group. State names are written on the map. A white dashed line marks the boundary between the two sides. Thin dark gray lines are railroads built by 1863. Diamonds mark battles, colored by who won: use the legend to read the result, because a battle's pop-up gives its name and dates but not the result. White diamonds are Inconclusive and gray circles are Other. Bigger diamonds mean more soldiers were killed, wounded, captured or missing. Tan shaded areas show the land each battlefield covered, and areas with diagonal stripes show where the fighting was heaviest.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. A nation divided

    On the map:

    1. Open the legend and find the groups for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863).
    2. Match each state's shade to its group.
    3. Find the state on the map that did not exist in 1861 (the layer shows the country in 1863).

    Answer: Which states left the Union before the attack on Fort Sumter in April 1861? Which left after? Which slave states stayed in the Union? Which state on the map did not exist in 1861?

  2. The border states

    On the map:

    1. Zoom in to Washington, D.C., on the east coast between Maryland and Virginia.
    2. Find the two states that border it.
    3. Check each one's shade in the legend.

    Answer: Which two states border Washington, D.C.? What would have happened to the capital if Maryland had left the Union?

  3. Railroads, North and South

    On the map:

    1. Find the white dashed boundary between the Union and the Confederacy.
    2. In Map layers, turn U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) off to see the railroad lines better.
    3. Compare the railroads (thin dark gray lines) north and south of the boundary.

    Answer: Which side had more railroads? Why would railroads matter in a war?

  4. Where were the battles?

    On the map:

    1. Zoom to Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania.
    2. Click the tan shaded areas of two battlefields and read their names.
    3. Use the legend to find a battlefield in a Union state.

    Answer: Where were most battles fought? Name a battle fought in a state the legend shows as a Union state.

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about the Civil War that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Subjects: US History, Geography, Civics, Economics. Grade: 8. Time: 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.

Learning objectives

Students will:

  • Sort the states on the 1863 map into those that seceded before Fort Sumter, those that seceded after, and the slave states that stayed in the Union, using the legend, and notice that the layer shows 1863, so West Virginia appears as a Union state that did not exist in 1861.
  • Locate Washington, D.C., identify the two states that border it, and explain from their legend shades why Maryland staying in the Union mattered.
  • Compare the density of railroads north and south of the Boundary between Union and Confederacy and say why that difference mattered in a war.
  • Find battlefields in Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania, read their names and sizes from the pop-ups, and identify which were fought in Union states.
  • Use evidence from at least two layers to explain how the geography of a divided nation shaped the Civil War.

  • Using a map legend

  • Front-of-class demonstration

  • Homework or flipped classroom

Before class

About this map: Every layer is on when the map opens and there are no bookmarks, so students zoom to Virginia, Washington, D.C., Maryland and Pennsylvania themselves. Battle pop-ups give the name and dates; the result is read from the legend.

Materials, ways to prepare and how every lesson works are on How these lessons work.

Discussion questions

  1. Most of the tan battlefield areas sit in Virginia, between Washington and Richmond. What about the map explains why so much of the fighting happened there?
  2. You compared railroad lines north and south of the boundary. What else, not shown on this map, would you want to know before deciding how big the Union's advantage really was?
  3. Antietam and Gettysburg are the biggest battlefield areas in Union states. Why might a Confederate army have crossed the boundary into Maryland and Pennsylvania, given what the map shows about the two sides?

Support and stretch

  • Support: Do question 1 together from the front with the legend open beside the map, and write the five group names on the board with one state each.
  • Stretch: Click the largest diamonds in Civil War Battlefields to read their names and dates, and ask whether the biggest battles lie near the boundary, on railroads, or both.

Common misunderstandings

  • “All slave states joined the Confederacy.” The legend shows five slave states that stayed in the Union: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri and West Virginia.
  • “The war was fought evenly across the North and the South.” Most battlefields on the map are in Confederate states, above all Virginia.

Name Date

Big question: Why did the Union need Vicksburg, and how did Grant take it?

Open the map: The Battle of Vicksburg

Before you start

In 1862, Union forces captured New Orleans and Memphis, two cities on the Mississippi River. Between the two, the Confederates still held part of the river, including the city of Vicksburg, Mississippi. In spring 1863, Union General Ulysses S. Grant set out to capture it.

Reading the map

The yellow pin is Vicksburg. Dark pins mark places on Grant's route, each with its name. City and state names, such as Jackson and Louisiana, are part of the basemap. Railroads are thin dark lines with short cross marks, like a track; they appear when you zoom in, and they include lines built after the war. Civil War Battlefields is off when the map opens: turn it on in Map layers. Its diamonds mark battles, colored by who won: use the legend to read the result, because a battle's pop-up gives its name and dates but not the result.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Why Vicksburg?

    On the map:

    1. Open The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark.
    2. Find Vicksburg, the yellow pin on the Mississippi River.
    3. Zoom in until the railroads appear and follow the line east from Vicksburg.
    4. Find Jackson, Mississippi, on the basemap (the state capital, east of Vicksburg).

    Answer: Why would both sides want Vicksburg?

  2. Grant's route

    On the map:

    1. Find the dark pins for Milliken's Bend, New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards.
    2. Check which side of the river each pin is on.
    3. Use Measure for the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend.

    Answer: Which side of the river is each place on? Why did Grant march south before crossing the river? Measure the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend: miles

  3. The battles of May 1863

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on Civil War Battlefields.
    2. Click the diamonds between Bruinsburg Bend and Vicksburg and read their dates.
    3. Click the diamonds east toward Jackson and read their dates.

    Answer: Which battles were fought between Bruinsburg Bend, Vicksburg and Jackson? List them in order by date.

  4. Splitting the Confederacy

    On the map:

    1. Zoom out until you can see the Mississippi River from Memphis to the Gulf of Mexico.
    2. Keep Civil War Battlefields on and click the diamond at Port Hudson, in Louisiana south of Vicksburg.
    3. Read when the siege of Port Hudson ended.
    4. Read the state names on the basemap.

    Answer: When did Port Hudson end? Which states lie west of the river? What could the Union control once Vicksburg and Port Hudson had both fallen?

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two places on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

What did the map show you about the Vicksburg campaign that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Learning objectives

Students will:

  • Locate Vicksburg on the Mississippi River and follow the railroad east to Jackson to explain why both sides wanted the city.

  • List the battles of the Vicksburg campaign in date order from the Civil War Battlefields pop-ups.

Discussion questions

  1. Grant marched his army down the far bank and crossed more than 30 miles south of the city. What on the map explains that choice, and what risks did it carry?
  2. Between Port Gibson on May 1 and the start of the siege on May 18, the battles run east toward Jackson and then back west. Why might Grant have gone to Jackson first instead of straight to Vicksburg?
  3. Zoomed out, the river runs from Memphis to the Gulf with Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas on the far side. How does the map help explain why Vicksburg's surrender, and not just Gettysburg, was a turning point of July 1863?

Before you start

In 1787, delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia and wrote the Constitution. Large and small states disagreed about how many votes each should have in Congress. They settled it with the Great Compromise, and with the Three-Fifths Compromise on how enslaved people were counted. The Constitution would take effect only when nine states had ratified it, each at a special convention.

Reading the map

The map has no place names: click a pie or a state to see its name in the pop-up title. Pies on the states show the people in 1790: blue for free, orange-red for enslaved, and bigger pies for more people. Three layers are off when the map opens. In House seats in 1793, darker blue means more seats, and each label gives the state's abbreviation and seats. In Ratifying the Constitution, each pie sits where a state's convention met: blue for votes to ratify, orange-red for votes against, and labels give the order each state ratified. Maine is shown within Massachusetts and West Virginia within Virginia.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Who lived where in 1790?

    On the map:

    1. Open The states in 1790 bookmark.
    2. Click the pies and read each pop-up.
    3. Read the first line of each pop-up, which gives the percentage enslaved.

    Answer: Which state had the most people? In which states were more than a quarter of the people enslaved?

  2. Seats in Congress

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on House seats in 1793.
    2. Read the labels: each gives the state and its seats, and darker blue means more seats.
    3. Click two states and read how many senators each had.

    Answer: Which state had the most seats in the House of Representatives, and which the fewest? How many senators did each of your two states have? Why do you think the House and the Senate are counted differently?

  3. The three-fifths clause

    On the map:

    1. Click Virginia and South Carolina.
    2. Read the seats in 1793 in each pop-up, then the last two lines: the seats if enslaved people had been counted in full, or not at all.
    3. Click other states and compare the same three numbers.

    Answer: Under the three-fifths clause, three of every five enslaved people were counted when House seats were shared out. How many seats did Virginia and South Carolina each have under the clause, and how many would each have had if enslaved people had been counted in full, or not at all? Which states gained seats by counting enslaved people, who could not vote? Virginia: seats with the three-fifths clause; if counted in full; if not counted at all.

  4. How close was ratification?

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn off Population in 1790 and House seats in 1793.
    2. Turn on Ratifying the Constitution.
    3. Click the pies and read the first line of each pop-up: the votes for and against.
    4. Find North Carolina and click both of its pies.

    Answer: Which three votes were closest? Why does North Carolina have two pies?

Discussion questions

  1. Virginia had the most people and the most House seats but the same two senators as Delaware. Looking at the pies and the seat labels, which states had most to gain from each half of that bargain?
  2. Compare the actual seats for Virginia and South Carolina with the two alternatives in their pop-ups. How many seats did the three-fifths clause move, and who in those states did that extra representation speak for?
  3. Some ratification votes were very close, and North Carolina voted twice. What does the map suggest might have happened if one or two of those votes had gone the other way?

Support and stretch

  • Support: Write the three layer names on the board and do question 2 together from the front, reading one pop-up aloud before pairs click their own states.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The three-fifths clause gave enslaved people a share of representation.” It gave slaveholding states more seats, not enslaved people a voice: they could not vote. Virginia's pop-up shows 19 seats under the clause, against 13 if enslaved people had not been counted.
  • “Every state ratified the Constitution easily.” Rhode Island ratified by 34 to 32 and New York by 30 to 27, and North Carolina's first convention did not ratify.
  • “Large states had more senators.” Every state had two senators; only House seats followed population.

    On the map:

    1. Zoom to your town; the basemap has place names.
    2. Find the blue lines, which are the boundaries of congressional districts.
    3. Click inside your district and read the pop-up.
    4. Zoom out to see your whole state.

    On the map:

    2. Find four public places, not homes: a courthouse, city hall, library, place of worship, polling place or newspaper office.
    3. Use Sketch to put a pin on each one.
    4. Next to each pin, write a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there.
    5. Finish in one lesson or take a screenshot, because sketches are not saved.

  3. Responsibilities

    On the map:

    1. Start at the courthouse or city hall you pinned.
    2. Add a pin at each place where people carry out a citizen's responsibility: voting, jury service, paying taxes.
    3. Next to each pin, write the responsibility.

Before you start

George Washington belonged to no party, and in 1796, as he prepared to leave office, he warned Americans against parties. By then two had formed: the Federalists, led by John Adams and Alexander Hamilton, and the Democratic-Republicans, led by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. Each elector cast two votes for president, and the runner-up became vice president.

Reading the map

The map has no place names: click a pie to see the state's name and its number of electors. Each pie shows how a state's electors voted: orange for John Adams (Federalist) and blue for Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican); use the legend. Bigger pies mean more electors. Each elector cast two votes; the pop-up lists the other candidates. Election of 1800 is off when the map opens. Pink squares mark two Supreme Court cases; each pop-up has a Why here part. Maine is shown within Massachusetts and West Virginia within Virginia, and territories aren't shown.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

    On the map:

    2. Use the legend to read the 1796 pies.
    3. Click each two-color pie and read its pop-up.

    2. Find the two-color pies.
    3. Click each one and read how its electors divided.

    Answer: Which states have two-color pies this time? How did each one's electors divide between Adams and Jefferson? Which state was the closest?

  3. Which states switched?

The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806

Compare the Louisiana Purchase with the United States of 1803, see why the Mississippi River and New Orleans mattered, and follow Lewis and Clark's route across rivers and biomes to the Pacific.

Inquiry

Compelling question

What did the Louisiana Purchase add to the United States, and why did the Mississippi River matter so much?

Pick the questions that suit your class: each one is answered from the map and says about how long it takes. The one marked If you only do one gets to the big question on its own in about 15 minutes. Under each question, From the front gives the exact clicks for teaching it on a projector. Answers and what to accept are linked under Teacher notes.

  1. A bigger country If you only do one About 12 minutes

    Open The Louisiana Purchase bookmark. Use the legend to compare the yellow Louisiana Purchase with the green land of 1783, and click the purchase for its size and price.

    From the front

    1. Open The Louisiana Purchase bookmark.
    2. Open the legend: green for the land of 1783, yellow for the Louisiana Purchase.
    3. Ask: about how much bigger did the country become?
    4. Click inside the yellow area and read the Notes in the pop-up.
    5. Ask: how much land was it, and what did it cost?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  2. Why New Orleans? About 15 minutes

    Turn on United States Watersheds. Click inside the two large brown outlines along the Ohio and the Missouri to name the regions, then follow the rivers on the basemap to find where their water reaches the sea, and explain why New Orleans mattered to western farmers.

    From the front

    1. In Map layers, turn on United States Watersheds.
    2. Click inside the large brown outline along the Ohio River and read the first line of the pop-up.
    3. Click inside the outline along the Missouri River and read its name.
    4. Zoom out and follow both rivers on the basemap to where their water reaches the sea.
    5. Ask: which big river do they flow into, and which city sits near its mouth?
    6. Ask: why did control of New Orleans matter to farmers west of the Appalachians?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  3. Up the Missouri About 10 minutes

    Open the Up the Missouri bookmark, follow the trail line and campsites upriver, turn off Watersheds and turn on Biomes, and click along the route for the biome's name.

    From the front

    1. Open the Up the Missouri bookmark.
    2. Trace the purple trail line and the campsite symbols up the Missouri River.
    3. In Map layers, turn off United States Watersheds and turn on Biomes.
    4. Click the shading along the route and read the first line of the pop-up.
    5. Ask: which biome covers the Great Plains?
    6. Ask: looking at where the campsites sit, why did the Corps travel along rivers?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  4. Across the Rockies About 12 minutes

    Open the Across the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark. Note where the trail leaves the yellow purchase, then measure the straight-line distance from the trail's eastern end at Pittsburgh to its western end on the Pacific coast.

    From the front

    1. Open the Across the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark.
    2. Follow the trail line west and point to where it leaves the yellow Louisiana Purchase.
    3. Ask: was the Pacific coast part of the purchase?
    4. Zoom out until the whole trail is on screen.
    5. Open Measure and click from the trail's eastern end at Pittsburgh to its western end on the Pacific coast.
    6. Ask: how does the straight-line distance compare with the trail's 4,900 miles?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Accept answers that give the purchase's size and price from the pop-up and use the watersheds, rivers or trail as evidence of what the land offered (rivers to the Gulf, plains, a route west) and why New Orleans and the Mississippi mattered to western farmers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; sketch pins for New Orleans and for two places on the trail, with notes (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them); or a short talk using the map. The question of whose land this was is in Looking back: the map has no Native nations layer, so it is answered from Before you start (the Corps met more than 50 Tribal Nations) and reasoning, not from the map.

The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: What did the Louisiana Purchase add to the United States, and why did the Mississippi River matter so much?

Open the map: The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806

Before you start

In 1803 the United States bought France's claim to a huge area west of the Mississippi River. Native nations lived on and governed most of that land; the National Park Service says the expedition met more than 50 Tribal Nations. President Thomas Jefferson sent the Corps of Discovery, led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, to explore it and look for a water route to the Pacific Ocean. The expedition set out in 1803 and returned in 1806.

Reading the map

The map has no place names: click an area to see its name. Use the legend: green is the land Britain gave up to the United States in 1783; yellow is the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. Edges of the purchase settled later have other colors or stripes. A purple line follows the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail, and small symbols mark the Corps' approximate campsites; the line and the symbols have no pop-ups. United States Watersheds and Biomes are off when the map opens and show today's landscape. Watersheds shows larger regions when you zoom out and smaller ones when you zoom in.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. A bigger country

    On the map:

    1. Open The Louisiana Purchase bookmark and use the legend.
    2. Compare the yellow Louisiana Purchase with the green land of the United States in 1783.
    3. Click the Louisiana Purchase and read its pop-up.

    Answer: About how much bigger did the country become? How much land was the Louisiana Purchase, and what did it cost? Size: about million acres. Price: $ million.

  2. Why New Orleans?

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on United States Watersheds.
    2. Click inside the two large brown outlines along the Ohio River and the Missouri River.
    3. Zoom out and follow the rivers on the map to where they end.

    Answer: Which river regions are the two outlines? Into which big river do they flow, and which city sits near its mouth? In 1800 farmers west of the Appalachians sent their crops to market by river: why did control of New Orleans matter to them?

  3. Up the Missouri

    On the map:

    1. Open the Up the Missouri bookmark.
    2. Follow the trail line and the campsite symbols up the Missouri River.
    3. In Map layers, turn off United States Watersheds and turn on Biomes.
    4. Click the shading along the route and read the first line of the pop-up.
    5. Look at where the campsites sit.

    Answer: Which biome covers the Great Plains? Why do you think the Corps traveled along rivers?

  4. Across the Rockies

    On the map:

    1. Open the Across the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark.
    2. Find where the trail line leaves the yellow Louisiana Purchase.
    3. Zoom out and find the trail's eastern end at Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, where the Ohio River begins.
    4. Use Measure for the straight-line distance from Pittsburgh to the trail's western end on the Pacific coast.

    Answer: Where does the trail line leave the Louisiana Purchase? Was the Pacific coast part of it? What is the straight-line distance from Pittsburgh to the Pacific end of the trail? Straight-line distance: miles. The trail itself is about 4,900 miles long.

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

The United States bought this land from France. Before you start says the Corps of Discovery met more than 50 Tribal Nations along the way. Whose land was it, and what does the map leave out?

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer and bookmark names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Subjects: US History, Geography, Indigenous Studies, Economics. Grade: 8. Time: 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.

Learning objectives

Students will:

  • Use the legend to compare the Louisiana Purchase with the land of 1783 and read the purchase pop-up for its size and price.
  • Use the United States Watersheds layer to name the Ohio and Missouri watersheds and trace on the basemap where their rivers reach the sea.
  • Follow the Lewis and Clark trail and campsites up the Missouri and use the Biomes layer to name the biomes the expedition crossed.
  • Find where the trail leaves the Louisiana Purchase and measure the straight-line distance from Pittsburgh to the Pacific coast.
  • Use the watershed boundaries and river routes as evidence to explain why New Orleans mattered to farmers west of the Appalachians.

Map skills

  • Using bookmarks to find places
  • Reading pop-ups
  • Using a map legend
  • Turning map layers on and off
  • Navigating a map
  • Measuring distances on a map
  • Sketching on a map

Ways to run this lesson

  • Front-of-class demonstration
  • 1:1 devices
  • Computer lab
  • Homework or flipped classroom

Before class

About this map: United States Watersheds and Biomes are off when the map opens; the territories, trail and campsites are on. The basemap has no place names, so students may need help finding Pittsburgh and New Orleans. The trail and campsite layers have no pop-ups.

Materials, ways to prepare and how every lesson works are on How these lessons work.

Discussion questions

  1. The purchase pop-up gives a price and an area. Looking at the watershed layer, what did the United States actually gain control of, and why was the river mouth worth more than the land?
  2. The map has layers for the purchase, the rivers and the expedition's campsites, but none for the Native nations who lived on and governed most of this land. Whose land was the Louisiana Purchase, and what would a layer showing them change about how you read the map?
  3. The trail runs well beyond the yellow purchase boundary before it reaches the Pacific. Using the distance you measured and the biomes you crossed, what does the route suggest about Jefferson's goals?

Support and stretch

  • Support: Do question 1 together from the front, write the three bookmark names on the board, and point out Pittsburgh and New Orleans on the basemap before pairs start question 2.
  • Stretch: With Biomes on, follow the trail from the Rockies to the coast, list each biome the Corps crossed, and explain how the landscape changed along the way.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The United States bought the land from the people who lived there.” It bought France's claim. Native nations lived on and governed much of the land, which the United States later took through treaties and force. The map has no layer of those nations; the National Park Service says the Corps met more than 50.
  • “Lewis and Clark explored only the Louisiana Purchase.” West of the Rocky Mountains the trail leaves the purchase: the Pacific Northwest was not part of it.
  • “The Louisiana Purchase was the state of Louisiana.” It stretched from the Gulf of Mexico to British North America, covering all or part of 15 of today's states.

Two layers, off when the map opens, show today's biomes and river basins along the route (modern reference data, not a historical reconstruction).

The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

Find where the War of 1812 was fought, see what Spain gave up in 1819, and compare Latin America's new nations with the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.

  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question

Inquiry

Compelling question

How did the War of 1812 and the years after it change the United States' place in North and South America?

Pick the questions that suit your class: each one is answered from the map and says about how long it takes. The one marked If you only do one gets to the big question on its own in about 15 minutes. Under each question, From the front gives the exact clicks for teaching it on a projector. Answers and what to accept are linked under Teacher notes.

  1. Where was the war fought? About 10 minutes

    Open The War of 1812 bookmark and use the battle diamonds to find the three main areas of fighting.

    From the front

    1. Open The War of 1812 bookmark.
    2. Open the legend: blue for an American victory, red for British, gray if inconclusive, and bigger diamonds for more casualties.
    3. Click a diamond near the Great Lakes and read the battle name and State Name in the pop-up.
    4. Click a diamond in each of the other clusters and read where it was fought.
    5. Ask: in which three areas was most of the fighting?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  2. The biggest battles If you only do one About 15 minutes

    Click the largest diamonds to find the battles with the most casualties, their dates and results, and compare the date of New Orleans with the Treaty of Ghent.

    From the front

    1. Open The War of 1812 bookmark.
    2. Click the biggest diamond and read Battle Dates, Battle Victor and Total Casualties in the pop-up.
    3. Click the next two biggest diamonds and read the same three fields.
    4. Ask: where and when was each battle fought, and who won?
    5. Write on the board: Treaty of Ghent signed December 24, 1814.
    6. Ask: which big battle came after the treaty was signed?

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  3. Florida and a new border About 12 minutes

    Open The 1819 boundary bookmark, turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and the Adams–Onís Treaty line, and read their pop-ups to describe what the treaty settled.

    From the front

    1. Open The 1819 boundary bookmark.
    2. In Map layers, turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819.
    3. Click the green land and read the Notes in the pop-up.
    4. Ask: what did the United States gain from Spain?
    5. Click part 1 of the pink dashed line and read its description, then click the next parts going west.
    6. Ask: which rivers and lines of latitude and longitude does the border follow?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  4. New nations and the Monroe Doctrine About 12 minutes

    Open Latin America in 1825, turn on the independence layer, and compare the dates of independence and US recognition with President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823.

    From the front

    1. Open the Latin America in 1825 bookmark.
    2. In Map layers, turn on Latin American independence and US recognition.
    3. Open the legend: blue circles recognized by 1824, orange diamonds recognized later.
    4. Click a blue circle and read the US recognition date in the pop-up.
    5. Write on the board: Monroe's message, December 2, 1823.
    6. Ask: which nations had the United States recognized before that date, and why might Monroe have warned European powers to stay out?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; a sketch of the three war fronts and of the 1819 border and the area the Monroe Doctrine covered (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them); or a short talk using the map. Accept answers that use the battles to show the war ended without gains, the 1819 layers to show the United States growing and fixing its border with Spain, and the independence layer to show the new nations the Monroe Doctrine spoke for.

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: How did the War of 1812 and the years after it change the United States' place in North and South America?

Open the map: The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

Before you start

In the early 1800s Britain and France were at war, and both seized American ships. British warships also forced sailors off American ships into the Royal Navy, and Britain supported Native nations resisting American settlement. In June 1812 the United States declared war on Britain.

Reading the map

The map has no place names: click a feature to see its name. Pink shading shows the United States in 1800. Diamonds mark battles; use the legend: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory, gray if neither side won; bigger diamonds mean more casualties. The legend says British for every opponent, but some battles were fought against Native nations: the pop-up's leaders and story tell you who fought. Each battle pop-up gives the dates, the victor and the casualties. Tan shading shows battlefield land. Three layers are off when the map opens: the land Spain gave up in 1819 (green), the treaty line (pink dashes, in seven parts) and the Latin American nations, shown as blue circles if the United States recognized them by 1824 and orange diamonds if later; the pop-up gives the exact date.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Where was the war fought?

    On the map:

    1. Open The War of 1812 bookmark.
    2. Click some diamonds in each group and read their pop-ups.

    Answer: In which three areas was most of the fighting?

  2. The biggest battles

    On the map:

    1. Click the three biggest diamonds.
    2. Read where and when each battle was fought, and who won.
    3. Compare each battle's date with December 24, 1814, when the peace treaty was signed at Ghent.

    Answer: Where and when was each battle fought, and who won? Which big battle came after the peace treaty?

  3. Florida and a new border

    On the map:

    1. Open The 1819 boundary bookmark.
    2. In Map layers, turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819.
    3. Click the green land and read its pop-up.
    4. Click each part of the pink dashed line and read its pop-up.

    Answer: What did the United States gain from Spain? Which rivers and lines of latitude and longitude does the new border follow?

  4. New nations and the Monroe Doctrine

    On the map:

    1. Open the Latin America in 1825 bookmark.
    2. Turn on Latin American independence and US recognition.
    3. Click the blue circles and read each recognition date in the pop-up.
    4. Check each date against December 2, 1823 (blue only means recognized by 1824).

    Answer: Which nations had the United States recognized before President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823? Why might Monroe have warned European powers to stay out of the Americas?

Your answer: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.

Looking back

What did the map show you about the War of 1812 and its results that you might not have noticed from reading alone?

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer and bookmark names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Subjects: US History, Geography, Government. Grade: 8. Time: 45 minutes, or 10–15 per question.

Learning objectives

Students will:

  • Use the battle diamonds in the Battles of the War of 1812 layer to identify the three main areas of fighting.
  • Click the largest diamonds to find the battles with the most casualties, their dates and results, and compare the date of New Orleans with the Treaty of Ghent.
  • Read the pop-ups of the Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line layers to describe what the treaty settled.
  • Compare the dates of independence and US recognition in the Latin American independence layer with Monroe's message of December 2, 1823.
  • Use the locations of the battles and the 1819 boundary as evidence to explain how the United States' position in North America changed between 1812 and 1823.

Map skills

  • Using bookmarks to find places
  • Reading pop-ups
  • Using a map legend
  • Navigating a map
  • Turning map layers on and off
  • Sketching on a map

Ways to run this lesson

  • Front-of-class demonstration
  • 1:1 devices
  • Computer lab
  • Homework or flipped classroom

Before class

About this map: When the map opens, the boundaries and battles are on and three layers are off: Land Spain gave up in 1819, Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819, and Latin American independence and US recognition. Students turn them on for questions 3 and 4.

Materials, ways to prepare and how every lesson works are on How these lessons work.

Discussion questions

  1. The battle diamonds cluster in three areas far apart. From the map, what was each side trying to control in each area, and why was none of them decisive?
  2. The Battle of New Orleans was fought after the Treaty of Ghent was signed. Looking at where Ghent and New Orleans are, what does that gap tell you about how news travelled and how wars ended in 1815?
  3. Most Latin American nations had declared independence before Monroe's 1823 message, and the United States recognized several of them. Comparing the dates on the map, was the Monroe Doctrine leading events or following them?

Support and stretch

  • Support: Do question 2 from the front, reading the three pop-up fields aloud, and keep the legend open on the board with the Treaty of Ghent date.
  • Stretch: Click the diamonds at Tippecanoe, Fort Mims and Horseshoe Bend, read who the leaders were, and explain why the legend's British label does not fit.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The United States won the War of 1812 and gained land.” The Treaty of Ghent returned the borders to where they were before the war, and the map shows American and British victories on every front.
  • “The Battle of New Orleans won the war.” It was fought on January 8, 1815, after the Treaty of Ghent was signed on December 24, 1814.
  • “Every battle was against British soldiers.” The battles in Alabama were part of the Creek War, fought against the Red Stick Creeks.
  • “Every blue circle was recognized before the Monroe Doctrine.” Blue means recognized by the end of 1824. Brazil and the Federation of Central America were recognized in 1824, after Monroe's message of December 2, 1823; the pop-up dates show it.

  • impressment
  • blockade
  • Treaty of Ghent
  • cession
  • boundary
  • recognition
  • Monroe Doctrine
  • independence
