Answer notes: 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicRoad to revolution and the Revolution
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • TX 8.10(C)
    • TX 8.4(C)
    • FL SS.8.A.3.6

Open map (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

1. Where did the war begin?

Open the Massachusetts bookmark and click the Lexington and Concord diamond, then the Boston diamond. Read the dates in each pop-up, and the winner from the diamond's color and the legend. Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

Where to find it on the mapMassachusetts bookmark. Lexington and Concord pop-up, the date line under the title: April 19, 1775. Legend (Revolutionary War Battles): blue diamond = American Victory, red = British Victory. Boston pop-up: April 19, 1775 to March 17, 1776, about 11 months. Measure tool, Boston to Concord: about 16 miles (accept 15 to 17).

NotesUse the Revolutionary War Battles legend for the result.

2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?

Zoom out until all 21 diamonds show, from Quebec to South Carolina. Click each one, read its dates, and sort the battles into two lists by year. Use the legend for the winner. Which colonies saw fighting each year, and what changed?

Where to find it on the mapRevolutionary War Battles layer, zoomed out to the whole east coast: 21 diamonds. Each pop-up's date line gives the year; the diamond color and the legend give the winner. The colony comes from the Thirteen British Colonies layer or the pop-up's account.

Accept answers thatA good answer names Massachusetts, New York and Virginia, and Quebec (a British province, not one of the thirteen colonies), for 1775 and adds North Carolina, South Carolina, New Jersey and Rhode Island for 1776, and says that the fighting began around Boston and then spread along the coast, with most battles from August 1776 in New York and New Jersey, where the British won nearly all of them.

Answer key
YearAmerican victoriesBritish victories
1775 (8 battles)American victories: Lexington and Concord, Boston (siege) and Gloucester (Massachusetts); Fort Ticonderoga and Crown Point (New York); Great Bridge (Virginia)British victories: Bunker Hill (Massachusetts); Quebec (Quebec)
1776 (13 battles)American victories: Moores Creek Bridge (North Carolina); Sullivan's Island and Breach Inlet (South Carolina); Gwynn's Island (Virginia); Trenton (New Jersey)British victories: Brooklyn, Valcour Island, Pell's Point, White Plains, Fort Washington (New York); Fort Lee, Mount Holly (New Jersey); Newport (Rhode Island)

3. Why New York?

Turn on Key Port Cities (it sits inside the Revolutionary War Battlefields group). Students use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port, name the major ports between Boston and Charleston (the layer has no pop-ups, so the battle diamonds and the coastline help), measure New York to Philadelphia and New York to Boston, and say what a navy based at New York could reach.

Where to find it on the mapKey Port Cities layer, legend: larger symbol = Major Port City, smaller = Port. Five major ports: Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Norfolk and Charleston, so the three between Boston and Charleston are New York, Philadelphia and Norfolk. The layer has no pop-ups or labels: New York sits by the Brooklyn diamond, Norfolk by the Great Bridge diamond, and Philadelphia is up the Delaware River south-west of Trenton. Measure tool: New York to Philadelphia about 80 miles (accept 75 to 85); New York to Boston about 190 miles (accept 180 to 200).

Accept answers thatA good answer names at least New York and Philadelphia, gives both distances within range, and uses the map to say that New York is a major port in the middle of the coast, about 80 miles from Philadelphia and 190 from Boston by Measure, so a navy based there could reach the other big ports and cut New England off from the colonies to the south.

NotesAccept Norfolk if a student works it out; it is the hardest to name without labels. Background for teachers: Battle of Brooklyn, American Battlefield Trust (opens in a new tab).

4. How did 1776 end?

Zoom in near New York City until the numbered turning points show, and follow circles 4 and 5. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton, and read the dates and the winner from the legend. Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton.

Where to find it on the mapTurning Points circles 4 (Fall of New York City, 1776, Victor: Britain) and 5 (Washington Strikes Back, 1776, Victor: United States); the pop-up's Battle details text tells the story of each. Revolutionary War Battles pop-ups: Fort Washington, November 16, 1776, and Fort Lee, November 20, 1776, red = British Victory; Trenton, December 26, 1776, blue = American Victory. Measure tool, New York City to Trenton: about 52 miles (accept 48 to 56).

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a route drawn with Sketch (not saved, so finish in one session or take a screenshot), or a short talk using the bookmark and the layers.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use dates and victors from the Revolutionary War Battles pop-ups and legend (Lexington and Concord, April 19, 1775, blue = American Victory; Fort Washington, November 16, 1776, red = British Victory; Trenton, December 26, 1776), the Major Port City symbol in the Key Port Cities legend, the Turning Points circles, and a Measure distance such as New York to Boston (about 190 miles).

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

The fighting moved from Boston to New York and then across New Jersey because the British went after the big port in the middle of the coast, which could cut New England off from the rest of the colonies, and the Americans fell back before striking at Trenton. On the Massachusetts bookmark, the Lexington and Concord pop-up gives April 19, 1775, and the legend shows its blue diamond means an American Victory; the Boston pop-up runs from April 19, 1775 to March 17, 1776, about 11 months. With Key Port Cities on, the legend's larger symbol marks New York as a Major Port City, and Measure gives about 190 miles to Boston and about 80 miles to Philadelphia, so a navy there could reach the other big ports. The pop-up dates put 13 battles in 1776, and red diamonds at Brooklyn, Fort Washington on November 16, 1776 and Fort Lee on November 20, 1776 show the British winning nearly all of them, until Trenton, December 26, 1776, with a blue diamond, about 52 miles from New York City by Measure. The pattern is that the fighting followed the coast and its ports, but my claim only covers 1775 and 1776, where the map ends.

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.

  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicWestward expansion and Manifest Destiny (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)

Open map (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?

1. Where did the trails begin?

Click three trails (use the legend to tell them apart) and note from each pop-up where the trail started and ended. Most began in Missouri: why there?

Where to find it on the mapTrails West pop-ups (title is the trail name, the text gives the places). Most trails start in Missouri: Independence (Oregon, California), St. Joseph (Pony Express), St. Louis (Butterfield Overland) or Missouri in general (Santa Fe). On the map, the Mormon Pioneer trail's eastern end is at Nauvoo, Illinois, on the Mississippi, and its pop-up mentions Nauvoo and Omaha.

Accept answers thatMissouri. For why, a good answer uses the map: Missouri was at the western edge of the settled states and on the Missouri River, so it was the last place to buy supplies and the river was the way in.

Answer key
TrailFromTo
OregonFrom: Independence, MissouriTo: Willamette River valley, near Portland, Oregon
CaliforniaFrom: Independence, Missouri, and Omaha, NebraskaTo: Northern California
Mormon PioneerFrom: Nauvoo, Illinois (the line's eastern end on the map), then past Omaha, NebraskaTo: Salt Lake City, Utah
Santa FeFrom: MissouriTo: Santa Fe, New Mexico
Pony ExpressFrom: St. Joseph, MissouriTo: Sacramento, California
Butterfield OverlandFrom: St. Louis, Missouri, and Memphis, Tennessee, via Fort Smith, ArkansasTo: San Francisco, California
Old SpanishFrom: Abiquiú, New MexicoTo: Los Angeles, California

2. How far, and how many?

Open the Oregon Trail pop-up for its length and how many people used it. Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri (on the basemap, just east of Kansas City), to Portland, Oregon, and compare it with the trail's length.

Where to find it on the mapOregon Trail pop-up: about 2,000 miles (3,219 km); 300,000 to 400,000 people between 1840 and 1860. Measure tool, Independence to Portland: about 1,500 miles (accept 1,450 to 1,550).

Accept answers thatThe trail is about 500 miles longer than the straight line. A good answer says the dotted line bends to follow rivers (the pop-up names the Platte, North Platte, Snake and Columbia) for water and grass, and crosses the mountains through passes rather than straight over them.

3. Whose land?

Turn on Indigenous Territories in Map layers and zoom in until the nations' names appear, then follow one trail from end to end. Was the West empty land when the trails were built? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?

Where to find it on the mapIndigenous Territories layer (off at start; names draw when zoomed in). Any trail runs through a continuous patchwork of shaded territories from Missouri to the coast; for example the Oregon Trail crosses lands labeled for the Kaw, Pawnee, Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Shoshone, Nez Perce and others. Accept any two names read from the map.

Accept answers thatNo, the land was not empty: the layer shows nations' territories along the whole trail. For the second part, a good answer reasons from the map that hundreds of thousands of travelers, their wagons and animals crossed these lands, so it could mean lost hunting grounds and grass, disease, pressure on water, forts and settlements along the route, and later loss of the land itself; any reasoned effect, positive or negative, that connects the trail to the people living there is acceptable.

4. From trails to rails

Turn on the Railroads group in Map layers. Using the legend, which trails does the Union Pacific and Central Pacific line follow most closely? Click a thin gray railroad line to see when it was in operation (the thick transcontinental lines have no pop-up).

Where to find it on the mapLegend: Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific) are thick colored lines running from Omaha across Nebraska, Wyoming, Utah and Nevada to Sacramento. Compare with the dotted California and Mormon Pioneer trails (and the Pony Express across Nevada). Railroads 1826 to 1911 pop-up: "Railroad in operation by:" followed by a year; any year the student reads is fine. The California Trail pop-up says the trail was used until 1869, when the transcontinental railroad was completed.

Accept answers thatThe California and Mormon Pioneer trails (also the Pony Express across Nevada). A good answer notes the railroad runs along the same river valleys and passes the wagon trails used, and gives a year read from a gray line's pop-up.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, one journey sketched on the map with notes (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the Trails West pop-ups (the Oregon Trail's about 2,000 miles and 300,000 to 400,000 people, 1840 to 1860; the California Trail used until 1869), Measure from Independence to Portland (about 1,500 miles), nations named on the Indigenous Territories layer, and the legend's Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and (Central Pacific) lines beside the dotted trails.

A model answer (level 4)

Trails and then railroads turned the West into a route for hundreds of thousands of settlers heading to Oregon, California and Utah, at the cost of the Indigenous nations whose lands the routes crossed. In the Trails West layer, the Oregon Trail pop-up says the trail was about 2,000 miles long and 300,000 to 400,000 people used it between 1840 and 1860, starting from Independence, Missouri. Measure from Independence to Portland, Oregon, gives about 1,500 miles, so the dotted line is about 500 miles longer because it follows rivers like the Platte and the Snake for water and grass. With the Indigenous Territories layer on and zoomed in, the Oregon Trail runs through lands labeled for the Pawnee, Lakota, Cheyenne and Shoshone, so the land was not empty, and those wagons and animals meant lost grass and hunting grounds. With Railroads on, the legend's Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and (Central Pacific) lines run from Omaha to Sacramento beside the California and Mormon Pioneer trails, and the California Trail pop-up says it was used until 1869, when the railroad was completed. The change over time is that the railroad replaced the wagon trails but kept the same route, so the same nations faced the pressure again.

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.

  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicReform and the road to war (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards

    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • FL SS.8.A.5.2

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did slavery divide the United States by 1850?

1. Free states and slave states

Use the legend for US States and Territories 1850 to tell the four groups apart (free, free by compromise, slave, slave by compromise), name a state in each, read two states' years from their pop-ups, and find the eastern line between free and slave states. The layer draws West Virginia separately and Missouri twice, so this question asks for groups and examples, not a count.

Where to find it on the mapLegend for US States and Territories 1850: four groups. Following the legend shades, the Free states group has 14 states; Iowa and California sit in the paler Free states and territories by compromise group. The Slave states group has 15 as drawn, counting West Virginia; Texas sits in the paler Slave states and territories by compromise group, and Missouri is drawn twice (once in each slave group), so accept 14 to 16 free and 14 to 16 slave with reasons. Pop-up title gives the state name; the first line gives the year (for example Pennsylvania 1780, Virginia 1788). In the East the shades change along the southern border of Pennsylvania and then the Ohio River.

Accept answers thatOne state correctly named for each of the four legend groups; two state years read from pop-ups; the eastern line described as the southern border of Pennsylvania and then the Ohio River. Do not mark on counts: the layer's groups make a count ambiguous.

Answer key
Legend groupStates as drawn
Free states (14)States as drawn: Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin
Free states and territories by compromiseStates as drawn: Iowa and California, plus Oregon, Minnesota and the unorganized territories
Slave states (15 as drawn)States as drawn: Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia (part of Virginia in 1850), North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky, Missouri
Slave states and territories by compromiseStates as drawn: Texas and Missouri (drawn a second time), plus New Mexico and Utah territories and the Indian Territory (drawn as Oklahoma)

NotesHistorically there were 15 free and 15 slave states in 1850 (Iowa and California free, Texas slave). The legend groups split them by how they became free or slave, so the counts students get depend on which groups they add together; the reasoning matters more than the number.

2. The Missouri Compromise

Find the Missouri Compromise Line (gray dashed) and click it for its pop-up. Which slave state lies mostly north of it, and why does that matter?

Where to find it on the mapMissouri Compromise Line pop-up: title Missouri Compromise Line (36°30′ North), year Enacted 1820, and a note that the line divided future slave and free states west of the Mississippi and that Missouri was the exception because most of it lies north of the parallel. On the map, Missouri (green, slave state shades) sits almost entirely north of the line.

Accept answers that1820; Missouri. A good answer says Missouri was allowed in as a slave state even though it lies north of the line, so the line was a deal, not a rule that applied everywhere, and it set up the argument over every new state and territory. Mentioning Maine as the free state admitted at the same time is extra.

3. The internal slave trade

Follow the solid black lines of Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade (turn Underground Railroad Approximate Routes off in Map layers to see them clearly). Click the states where the lines begin and where they come together to read their names. Where do the lines reach the coast? The lines have no arrows, so students infer the direction from the pattern and what they have learned.

Where to find it on the mapInternal Routes of the US Slave Trade, solid black lines (no pop-up). Reading them against the state pop-ups: several lines start in Virginia (one from near the Ohio border and one from Kentucky join them), one starts in North Carolina, and they run south and west to meet in central Alabama and at the Mississippi coast in Louisiana. They reach the coast at New Orleans and the Gulf (Louisiana, Alabama) and on the Atlantic off South Carolina.

Accept answers thatA good answer names Virginia (and Kentucky or North Carolina) at one end and Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana, with New Orleans on the Gulf, at the other, and says the lines join up as they head south and west toward the ports. From that pattern and from class, students should say enslaved people were moved from the older Upper South to the Deep South and the Gulf, where cotton and sugar plantations wanted labor; accept any direction argued from the map plus a reason.

4. Routes to freedom

Open the Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark and follow the orange Underground Railroad routes north from the Ohio River; the Cities labels appear when zoomed in. Where do they lead, and why do many continue to Canada?

Where to find it on the mapIllinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark; Underground Railroad Approximate Routes (orange lines) and Cities (orange dots in the US, black dots in Canada; labels draw when zoomed in). Routes run north across Ohio, Indiana and Illinois to Lake Erie and the Detroit River, at Cleveland, Ashtabula, Toledo and Detroit, and on to the black dots at Chatham and Toronto (Ontario) and Montreal (Quebec).

Accept answers thatNorth to the Great Lakes and across into Canada. A good answer gives two or three town names from the map and explains that freedom seekers were not safe in free states (after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 they could be captured and returned), so Canada, outside the United States, was the safer end of the route.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a sketch that marks free and slave states and one route (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the four legend groups and state pop-up years from US States and Territories 1850 (Pennsylvania 1780, Virginia 1788), the line along the southern border of Pennsylvania and the Ohio River, the Missouri Compromise Line pop-up (Enacted 1820), the black Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade from Virginia to New Orleans, and the orange Underground Railroad routes north to Canada.

A model answer (level 4)

By 1850 slavery divided the United States into a free North and a slave South, with a line that every new state and every escape route had to cross. The legend for US States and Territories 1850 has four groups, and the pop-ups give each state's year: Pennsylvania 1780 in the Free states group and Virginia 1788 in the Slave states group. In the East the shade changes along the southern border of Pennsylvania and then the Ohio River, so a river marked the divide. The Missouri Compromise Line pop-up says Enacted 1820 and that Missouri was the exception because most of it lies north of the parallel, so the division was a deal, not a rule. With the Underground Railroad layer off, the black Internal Routes of the US Slave Trade start in Virginia and join up heading south and west to New Orleans, so enslaved people were moved from the Upper South to the Deep South for plantation labor. From the Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio bookmark, the orange Underground Railroad routes run north past Cleveland and Detroit to the black dots at Chatham and Toronto in Canada, because after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 free states were unsafe. One limit is that the layers were traced from a 1920 atlas, so the routes are approximate.

Answer notes: Civil War Battlefields

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.

  • TopicThe Civil War (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)

Open map (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did the geography of a divided nation shape the Civil War, as the map shows the country in 1863?

1. A nation divided

Use the legend for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) to sort the states: which seceded before Fort Sumter, which after, and which slave states stayed in the Union? Then spot the state on this 1863 layer that did not exist in 1861 (West Virginia), as the way in to how the map's date matters.

Where to find it on the mapLegend for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863): the groups are Union Free State, Union slave state (border state), Slave state seceding before Fort Sumter, April 1861, Slave state seceding after Fort Sumter, April 1861, and Territories. State names are labels on the layer; zoom in if a label is hidden. Counts from the layer: 7 before, 4 after, 5 border states. West Virginia (admitted June 20, 1863) is the state that did not exist in 1861; in 1861 its counties were part of Virginia, which seceded.

Answer key
GroupStates on the map
Seceded before Fort Sumter (7)States on the map: South Carolina, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Texas
Seceded after Fort Sumter (4)States on the map: Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, Tennessee
Union slave states, the border states (5)States on the map: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri, West Virginia
Union free states (19)States on the map: Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, Kansas, California, Oregon

NotesWest Virginia split from Virginia and joined the Union as a state in June 1863, which is why it appears on this 1863 map. The two Union shades are close (dark blue and lighter blue), so students may need the legend side by side with the map.

2. The border states

Zoom to Washington, D.C. Which two states border it? Using the legend shades of those two states, what would have happened to the capital if Maryland had left the Union?

Where to find it on the mapZoom to the District of Columbia (a small unshaded area labeled on the States layer). Its neighbors are Maryland (legend: Union slave state, border state) and Virginia (legend: Slave state seceding after Fort Sumter). The white dashed Boundary between Union and Confederacy runs right past the capital.

Accept answers thatMaryland and Virginia. A good answer uses the legend to say Virginia had seceded, so if Maryland had left too, Washington would have been surrounded by Confederate states and cut off from the rest of the Union.

3. Railroads, North and South

Compare the Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static) layer (thin dark gray lines) north and south of the Boundary between Union and Confederacy (a white dashed line). Turning the States layer off in Map layers makes the lines easier to see. Which side had more railroads, and why would that matter in a war?

Where to find it on the mapRailroads 1826 to 1863 (static) layer and the Boundary between Union and Confederacy line (legend: white dashed). The lines are visibly denser north of the boundary, above all between the Mississippi River and the Atlantic coast. The map shows lines, not mileage.

Accept answers thatThe North (Union side). A good answer says a denser network let the Union move soldiers, food and weapons faster and farther, keep armies supplied, and shift troops between fronts; the South had fewer lines and gaps between them.

4. Where were the battles?

Zoom to Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania, and click the tan battlefield areas for names, sizes and state. Where were most battles fought, and which were fought in Union states (check the state's shade in the legend)?

Where to find it on the mapCivil War Battlefield Boundary pop-ups: the title is the battle name; Battlefield Acres and State Name (two-letter code) are listed below. Most tan areas are in Virginia (the layer has far more in VA than in any other state). Union states by the legend: Maryland (border state) has Antietam (34,937 acres), South Mountain, Monocacy, Boonsboro, Williamsport, Hancock and Folck's Mill; Pennsylvania (Union free state) has Gettysburg (73,551 acres) and Hanover. If a pop-up says 1 of 2, a core area sits under the boundary; use the arrows.

Accept answers thatMost battles were in the Confederate states, above all Virginia, between the two capitals. Any battle named from a Maryland or Pennsylvania pop-up, most often Antietam or Gettysburg.

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a sketch of the front line with notes (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

A model answer (level 4)

The geography of a divided nation shaped the Civil War by putting the Union capital right on the front line, giving the North a much denser railroad network, and making Virginia the place where most of the fighting happened. Zoomed to Washington, D.C., the legend shows Maryland as a Union slave state, a border state, and Virginia as a slave state seceding after Fort Sumter, with the white dashed Boundary between Union and Confederacy running right past the capital, so if Maryland had left too, Washington would have been surrounded. With the States layer off, the thin dark gray lines of Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static) are clearly denser north of the boundary, between the Mississippi River and the Atlantic coast, so the Union could move soldiers, food and weapons faster and farther. The Civil War Battlefield Boundary pop-ups put far more tan areas in Virginia than in any other state, between Washington and Richmond, while in Union states they give Antietam in Maryland at 34,937 acres and Gettysburg in Pennsylvania at 73,551 acres. The pattern is that the battles cluster along the boundary between the two capitals, but the map shows 1863, so West Virginia appears as a Union state even though in 1861 it was part of Virginia.

Answer notes: The Battle of Vicksburg

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.

  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicThe Civil War
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map

Open map (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

Why did the Union need Vicksburg, and how did Grant take it?

1. Why Vicksburg?

Open The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark. Vicksburg is the yellow pin. Look at where it sits on the Mississippi River. Zoom in until the railroads draw and follow the line east from Vicksburg to Jackson, Mississippi, the state capital, which is a basemap label (not a pin). Why would both sides want the city?

Where to find it on the mapThe Battle of Vicksburg bookmark; yellow pin at Vicksburg on a bend of the Mississippi; Railroads 1826 to 1911 layer, which draws when zoomed in to about 1:1,500,000 or closer; Jackson is a label on the Modern Antique basemap about 40 miles east.

Accept answers thatA good answer says Vicksburg sits on the river, so whoever held it controlled traffic on the Mississippi, and that its railroad linked the river to Jackson and the rest of the Confederacy, so it was both a river stronghold and a rail junction. Mentioning the bluffs or guns is extra, not on the map.

2. Grant's route

Find the dark pins and put them in order along Grant's route: Milliken's Bend, New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend, then Edwards. Which side of the river is each on? Measure the straight-line distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend.

Where to find it on the mapKey Places in the Union March to Vicksburg pins, read against the river and the basemap state labels: Milliken's Bend, New Carthage and Hard Times are on the west (Louisiana) bank; Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards are on the east (Mississippi) side. Measure tool, Milliken's Bend pin to Bruinsburg Bend pin: about 33 miles in a straight line (accept 31 to 36).

Accept answers thatA good answer notices that Vicksburg's pin sits on the river between Milliken's Bend (north) and Bruinsburg Bend (south), so Grant could not cross right at the city; he marched down the far bank, out of reach of the city, crossed well to the south, then turned back toward Vicksburg from the east (Edwards).

3. The battles of May 1863

Turn on Civil War Battlefields in Map layers and click the diamonds between Bruinsburg Bend and Vicksburg, and east toward Jackson. Put the battles in order by date from the pop-ups.

Where to find it on the mapCivil War Battlefields pop-ups: the name is in bold and the dates below it. Port Gibson's pop-up says 1 of 2; both entries are the same battle. Grand Gulf (April 29, 1863), on the river just north of Bruinsburg, is the Union navy's failed attack before the crossing; accept it if students include it.

RaymondDates: May 12, 1863
Jackson, MississippiDates: May 14, 1863

VicksburgDates: May 18, 1863 – July 4, 1863

4. Splitting the Confederacy

Zoom out to see the whole Mississippi River from Memphis to the Gulf. With Civil War Battlefields on, click the diamond at Port Hudson, Louisiana, south of Vicksburg, for its dates. Using the state names on the basemap, which states lie west of the river, and what did the Union control once both Vicksburg and Port Hudson had surrendered?

Where to find it on the mapCivil War Battlefields pop-up for Port Hudson: May 21, 1863 – July 9, 1863. Vicksburg pop-up: May 18, 1863 – July 4, 1863. Basemap state labels west of the river: Louisiana (most of it), Arkansas, Texas (and Missouri further north, Union side).

Accept answers thatPort Hudson surrendered on July 9, 1863, five days after Vicksburg. A good answer names Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas west of the river and says the Union then controlled the whole Mississippi, so those Confederate states were cut off from the rest of the Confederacy and the river was open to Union ships and closed to Confederate supplies.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, Grant's route sketched on the map (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the yellow Vicksburg pin on the Mississippi and the railroad east to the Jackson basemap label, the dark Key Places pins in order (Milliken's Bend to Edwards) with Measure from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend (about 33 miles), and dates from the Civil War Battlefields pop-ups (Port Gibson, May 1, 1863; Vicksburg, May 18, 1863 – July 4, 1863; Port Hudson, to July 9, 1863).

A model answer (level 4)

The Union needed Vicksburg because it controlled the Mississippi River and a railroad into the Confederacy, and Grant took it by marching around the city to attack from the east. On The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark the yellow pin sits on a bend of the Mississippi, and zoomed in, the Railroads 1826 to 1911 line runs east to the Jackson label on the basemap, so it was a river stronghold and a rail junction. The dark Key Places pins show Grant's route: Milliken's Bend, New Carthage and Hard Times on the Louisiana bank, then Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards on the east side. By Measure, Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend is about 33 miles, so Grant crossed well south instead of attacking straight across. With Civil War Battlefields on, the pop-up dates run from Port Gibson, May 1, 1863, through Raymond, Jackson and Champion Hill to Big Black River Bridge, May 17, and the Vicksburg pop-up gives May 18, 1863 – July 4, 1863, a siege of about six weeks. Zoomed out, the Port Hudson pop-up ends July 9, 1863, and the basemap shows Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas west of the river, so the Union held the whole river and those states were cut off. One limit is that the railroad layer includes lines built after the war.

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.

  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicConfederation and the Constitution (also fits: The early republic)

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did the Constitution balance large and small states, and how close did it come to being rejected?

1. Who lived where in 1790?

Open The states in 1790 bookmark. Students compare the pie sizes to find the most populous state, then click the pies and read the 1790 census line of each pop-up to find the states where more than a quarter of the people were enslaved.

Where to find it on the mapThe states in 1790 bookmark; Population in 1790 layer. Biggest pie and pop-up first line: Virginia, 747,610 people (Kentucky is counted separately; Massachusetts, which then included Maine, is next with 475,327). The percentage in the first line of each pop-up ("1790 census: … people, … of them enslaved (…%)") is above 25 in five states, listed below. Legend: blue = free people, orange-red = enslaved people.

2. Seats in Congress

Turn on House seats in 1793. Students use the labels (abbreviation and seats) and the legend to find the states with the most and fewest seats, then read the pop-up to compare House seats with senators.

Where to find it on the mapHouse seats in 1793 layer. Labels and legend (darkest class, 13 to 19 seats): Virginia, VA: 19, the most of the 105 seats. Palest class (1 to 2 seats): Delaware, DE: 1, the fewest; Vermont, Rhode Island, Kentucky and Georgia have 2. Pop-up, third line: "plus 2 senators, like every state".

Accept answers thatA good answer names Virginia (19) and Delaware (1), says every state had two senators, and explains the Great Compromise in its own words: House seats follow population, which suited the large states, while the equal Senate protected the small ones. The pop-up also gives the ratio, one seat for every 33,000 people counted.

3. The three-fifths clause

Students click Virginia and South Carolina and read the last two lines of each pop-up, which give the seats each would have had if enslaved people had been counted in full or not at all, and compare them with the actual seats. Then they look for other states where the two numbers differ.

Where to find it on the mapPopulation in 1790 or House seats in 1793 pop-up, the lines "That gave … House seats in 1793", "If enslaved people had been counted in full" and "If they had not been counted at all". Virginia: 19, 22, 13. South Carolina: 6, 7, 4. Seven states show a higher seat count under the clause than with no count, listed below.

Accept answers thatA good answer gives Virginia 19, 22 and 13 (fill-in) and South Carolina 6, 7 and 4, names at least Virginia, North Carolina, Maryland and South Carolina as states that gained seats, and says that enslaved people were counted for seats but could not vote, so the gain went to the slaveholding states. The seven states gained 15 seats in all (105 instead of 90), Virginia alone 6.

4. How close was ratification?

Turn off Population in 1790 and House seats in 1793 and turn on Ratifying the Constitution. Students click the pies, read the vote line of each pop-up ("Ratified on …: … for, … against") to find the three closest votes, and open both North Carolina pies to explain why there are two.

Where to find it on the mapRatifying the Constitution layer; legend: blue = voted to ratify, orange-red = voted against. Pop-up first line: Rhode Island 34 for, 32 against (label RI 13, May 29, 1790); New York 30–27 (NY 11, July 26, 1788); Massachusetts 187–168 (MA 6, February 6, 1788). By number of votes the next closest are Virginia 89–79 (VA 10) and New Hampshire 57–47 (NH 9, the ninth state, enough to put the Constitution into effect). North Carolina: the NC (1788) pie at Hillsborough, titled "Did not ratify (first convention)", 83 for, 184 against, with a note that a second convention ratified in November 1789; the NC 12 pie at Fayetteville, 194–77, November 21, 1789.

Accept answers thatA good answer names Rhode Island, New York and Massachusetts (accept Virginia or New Hampshire if the student counts the gap in votes rather than the share), and explains that North Carolina's first convention did not ratify and a second one did more than a year later, after Congress had proposed the Bill of Rights. Sources differ on the exact 1788 vote and date; accept the pop-up's figures.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; sketch pins for James Madison, Alexander Hamilton, Patrick Henry and George Mason, each with a quote and the principle it argues about (sketches are not saved, so finish in one session or take a screenshot); or a short talk using the map.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the House seats in 1793 labels, legend and pop-ups (Virginia VA: 19, Delaware DE: 1, and 2 senators for every state), the three-fifths lines of a pop-up (Virginia 19 seats, 22 if counted in full, 13 if not counted), and the vote line of the Ratifying the Constitution pop-ups (Rhode Island 34–32 on May 29, 1790; New York 30–27; Massachusetts 187–168).

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

The Constitution balanced large and small states by giving each state House seats by population but the same two senators, and it came very close to being rejected in small Rhode Island and in big New York and Massachusetts. In the House seats in 1793 layer, the label and the darkest legend class show Virginia with 19 seats, the most, while the palest class shows Delaware with only 1, yet the pop-up for each says plus 2 senators, like every state. That suited the large states in the House and protected the small ones in the Senate. The Virginia pop-up also shows the three-fifths clause at work: 19 seats, but only 13 if enslaved people had not been counted, so slaveholding states gained seats for enslaved people, who could not vote. In the Ratifying the Constitution layer, the vote line of the pop-ups shows how close it was: Rhode Island 34 to 32 on May 29, 1790, New York 30 to 27 on July 26, 1788, and Massachusetts 187 to 168 on February 6, 1788. North Carolina even has two pies, because its first convention at Hillsborough in 1788 did not ratify and a second one did in November 1789. The pattern is that a small state like Delaware ratified first and unanimously, 30 to 0 on December 7, 1787, while the closest votes came in the smallest state, Rhode Island, and in two of the biggest, New York and Massachusetts, so the balance held, but only just.

Answer notes: Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicConfederation and the Constitution (also fits: The early republic)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Civ.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.Civ.8.6-8
    • C3 D2.Geo.1.6-8
    • TX 8.19(B)
    • TX 8.19(C)
    • FL SS.8.CG.2.5

Open map (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

Where in our community do people use their rights and carry out their responsibilities?

1. Who represents us?

Students zoom to their town on the Topographic basemap and click inside their congressional district to read the pop-up, which names the representative, their party and the district number. Then they zoom out to the whole state and count the blue-outlined districts.

Where to find it on the mapCongressional districts (119th Congress) pop-up: "[Representative Name] ([Party]) represents [State] Congressional District [number]". The district count is the number of blue-outlined areas in the state when zoomed out, which equals the state's House seats after the 2020 census: for example California 52, Texas 38, Florida 28; six states (Alaska, Delaware, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming) have one, shown as the whole state.

Accept answers thatAccept the name and party as the pop-up gives them for the 119th Congress (2025–2027); a seat that has changed hands since the layer was updated may differ. In California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas and Utah the district on the November 2026 ballot may differ from the one shown (see the map's description).

2. Rights in public places

Students zoom in on their town until the Topographic basemap labels buildings, pick four public places it shows or that they know (courthouse, city hall, library, place of worship, polling place, newspaper office), sketch a pin on each and label it with a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there. Sketches are not saved, so students finish in one session or take a screenshot.

Where to find it on the mapThe Topographic basemap labels schools, churches, courthouses, libraries and city halls in most towns at close zoom. Sketch tool: a pin and a text label at each place. There is no stored answer; the teacher checks the student's screen or screenshot.

Accept answers thatFour pins on public places (not homes), each paired with a right that fits: a newspaper office with freedom of the press, a place of worship with free exercise of religion, city hall or a public square with assembly and petition, a library with speech and the press, a courthouse with due process or a jury trial (Fifth, Sixth and Seventh Amendments). A polling place connects with voting, which later amendments protect (15th, 19th and 26th), so accept it with that note.

3. Responsibilities

Students start from the courthouse or city hall they pinned in question 2, add pins for places where people carry out responsibilities as citizens (voting, jury service, paying taxes), and sort the responsibilities into required by law and voluntary.

Where to find it on the mapSketch pins on the student's map, usually at the courthouse (jury service), a polling place such as a school, library or church (voting), and a post office or tax office (paying taxes). There is no stored answer; check the screen or screenshot.

Accept answers thatAt least two pins with a responsibility each, and a sort that puts obeying laws, paying taxes, jury service when called and, for most men aged 18 through 25, Selective Service registration under required by law, and voting, staying informed, volunteering and attending community meetings under voluntary. Accept the point that voting is both a right and a responsibility, but no federal law requires it.

4. History where we live

Turn on National Register of Historic Places, zoom in until the diamonds appear, and click the two nearest the school. The pop-up gives the address but not the name, so students match the diamond to the basemap label or follow the pop-up's National Archive Information link. Look for a public building and the right or responsibility it connects with.

Where to find it on the mapNational Register of Historic Places layer, on at close zoom. Pop-up: address, city, county, state, resource type and a National Archive Information link; the place name is not shown, so students read it from the basemap label or the National Archives record. Legend: diamond colors for building, structure, district, site and object. If nothing is listed nearby, zoom out to the nearest town.

Accept answers thatTwo places identified by address or name, with a sensible link for any public building: a courthouse with jury service and a fair trial; a post office or newspaper building with sharing news and ideas; a school or library with staying informed. Accept "neither is a public building" with a reason.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from their own map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a screenshot of the sketched map with a short caption, or a short talk using the map. Sketches are not saved between sessions.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers name places on the student's own map: the representative, party and district number from the Congressional districts (119th Congress) pop-up; public buildings the Topographic basemap labels at close zoom (courthouse, city hall, library, polling place) with the student's Sketch pins; and a National Register of Historic Places diamond identified by its pop-up address and legend type.

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

In my town, people use their rights and carry out their responsibilities mostly in a few public buildings near the center: the courthouse, the library and the school that serves as a polling place. When I zoomed in on the Topographic basemap until it labeled buildings, I put a Sketch pin on the county courthouse on Main Street, labeled with the right to a jury trial, because that is where trials happen and where people do jury service when called, which is required by law. My second pin is the public library two blocks away, labeled freedom of speech and the press, because anyone can read and share ideas there. My third pin is my school, our polling place, where people vote; voting is a right and a responsibility, but no federal law requires it. The Congressional districts pop-up named my representative, their party and our district number, and when I zoomed out the blue outline covered far more than my town, so my representative speaks for many other places too. With National Register of Historic Places on, the diamond nearest my school had a Main Street address in its pop-up and the legend showed it was a building; the basemap label said it was the old courthouse, so rights have been used in the same place for a long time. One limit is that the map only shows buildings, and some responsibilities, like obeying laws, happen everywhere.

Answer notes: Political Parties and Federal Power, 1796–1819

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.

  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicThe early republic
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Civ.4.6-8

Open map (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did the first political parties divide the country?

1. The election of 1796

Open The sixteen states bookmark. Use the pies and the legend to find which regions mostly voted for Adams and which for Jefferson, and click the two-color pies for the split states' numbers.

Where to find it on the mapThe sixteen states bookmark; Election of 1796: electors' votes layer. Legend: orange = John Adams, blue = Thomas Jefferson; the pop-up names the state. All-orange pies: Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont. All-blue: Georgia, Kentucky, South Carolina, Tennessee. Two-color pies, from the pop-up's 1796 votes line: Maryland (Adams 7, Jefferson 4), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 14, Adams 1), Virginia (Jefferson 20, Adams 1), North Carolina (Jefferson 11, Adams 1).

Accept answers thatAdams: New England and the states around New York (New York, New Jersey, Delaware). Jefferson: the South and the West, plus most of Pennsylvania. The four split states named, with Maryland the only split state Adams won.

NotesThe totals are not on the map: Adams 71, Jefferson 68, so Jefferson, the runner-up, became vice president.

2. The election of 1800

Turn off Election of 1796 and turn on Election of 1800. Find the two-color pies and click each for the numbers; identify the closest state.

Where to find it on the mapElection of 1800: electors' votes layer; two-color pies, pop-up 1800 votes line: Maryland (Jefferson 5, Adams 5), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 8, Adams 7), North Carolina (Jefferson 8, Adams 4). Closest: Maryland, an even split.

NotesTotals, not on the map: Jefferson 73, Burr 73, Adams 65. Each elector cast two votes, so the pop-ups also list Burr and Charles C. Pinckney.

3. Which states switched?

Compare the two elections by switching between Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 in Map layers. Find the state whose whole pie changed color, the states whose shares changed, and describe where each party was strong.

Where to find it on the mapElection of 1796 and Election of 1800 layers, pop-up title (state and number of electors) and votes lines. New York, 12 electors: all Adams in 1796, all Jefferson in 1800. Shares changed: Maryland (Adams 7–4 to 5–5), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 14–1 to 8–7), North Carolina (Jefferson 11–1 to 8–4), Virginia (Jefferson 20–1 to 21–0). No New England state changed: Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont stayed all orange.

Accept answers thatNames New York as the only state that switched entirely; notes that the middle states (Maryland, Pennsylvania, North Carolina) were split in both elections; says the Federalists were strong in New England and the Democratic-Republicans in the South and West, with the middle states (and New York) deciding the result.

NotesNew York's 12 votes were more than the margin: without that switch Adams would have had 77 votes to Jefferson's 61 in 1800, instead of 65 to 73.

4. The Supreme Court, near the capital

Click the two pink squares and read Why here to find what happened in each place; measure the straight-line distance between them and ask why both cases arose so close to the capital.

Where to find it on the mapLandmark Supreme Court cases layer. Marbury v. Madison pop-up, Why here: William Marbury asked the Supreme Court in Washington for an order to get his commission. McCulloch v. Maryland pop-up, Why here: Maryland sued James McCulloch, cashier at the Baltimore branch of the Bank of the United States, to collect its tax on the bank. Measure tool, Baltimore square to Washington square: about 35 miles (accept 32 to 38).

Accept answers thatAny sensible link between the places and federal power: the Court and the federal government sat in Washington, so a dispute over a federal appointment began there; the Bank of the United States had a branch in nearby Baltimore, and Maryland's tax on it set state law against federal law.

NotesThe pop-ups also give the ruling and Why it matters: Marbury established judicial review (the pop-up quotes "A Law repugnant to the Constitution is void"); McCulloch held that Congress could charter the bank and that federal law is supreme over state law, so Maryland's tax was void. Marbury grew out of the change of party in 1801: Marbury was one of John Adams's last-minute appointments, and Jefferson's administration did not deliver his commission.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; a sketch that marks each party's region (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them); or sketch pins for the First Bank of the United States (Philadelphia, 1791) and Washington's Farewell Address (published in Philadelphia, 1796), with notes. Accept answers that name a region for each party, use the split states or New York's switch as evidence, and connect the parties to a dispute over federal power (the bank, the courts).

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the pies and legend of the Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 layers (orange for Adams, blue for Jefferson) with numbers from the pop-up votes lines, such as New York's 12 electors switching from all Adams to all Jefferson, Maryland 7–4 then 5–5 and Pennsylvania 14–1 then 8–7, and the Why here parts of the Supreme Court pop-ups with a Measure distance of about 35 miles.

Answer notes: The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • Time45 minutes, or 10–15 per question
  • TopicThe early republic (also fits: Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • TX 8.10(C)
    • TX 8.6(B)
    • FL SS.8.A.3.14

Open map (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

What did the Louisiana Purchase add to the United States, and why did the Mississippi River matter so much?

1. A bigger country

Open The Louisiana Purchase bookmark. Use the legend to compare the yellow Louisiana Purchase with the green land of 1783, and click the purchase for its size and price.

Where to find it on the mapThe Louisiana Purchase bookmark; Territorial acquisitions to 1803 layer. Legend: green = Territory of the Original Thirteen States (Ceded by Great Britain) 1783, yellow = Louisiana Purchase 1803. Louisiana Purchase 1803 pop-up, Notes: 530,000,000 acres, bought from France in 1803 for $15 million. Fill-in: 530 million acres, $15 million.

Accept answers thatAbout double, or roughly the same size as the country before it. The pop-up's Area in Square Kilometers field confirms it: about 2.1 million km² for the purchase and 2.3 million km² for the 1783 land.

NotesSome edges were settled later and have their own legend entries and pop-ups: the strip ceded to Great Britain in 1818 (striped), and the parts that came with Texas in 1845 and the Mexican Cession in 1848.

2. Why New Orleans?

Turn on United States Watersheds. Click inside the two large brown outlines along the Ohio and the Missouri to name the regions, then follow the rivers on the basemap to find where their water reaches the sea, and explain why New Orleans mattered to western farmers.

Where to find it on the mapUnited States Watersheds layer, at the bookmark's scale (zoomed out, the brown outlines are the largest regions; if the pop-up says 1 of 2, the region is the entry whose HUC ID has two digits). Pop-up, first line: Ohio Region (Kentucky, Ohio, Indiana and nearby states) and Missouri Region (the Great Plains). On the basemap both rivers join the Mississippi, which reaches the Gulf of Mexico at New Orleans; the city is not labeled, so students find the river mouth. Also accept Upper Mississippi Region or Arkansas-White-Red Region if clicked.

Accept answers thatNames both regions; says their rivers flow into the Mississippi and so past New Orleans to the sea; explains that whoever held New Orleans could stop or tax western farmers' crops on the way to market, so the United States needed the port.

NotesZoomed in, the layer shows smaller watersheds with their own names; ask students to zoom out until the outlines are the large regions. In 1802 Spanish officials at New Orleans stopped Americans storing goods in the port, and Jefferson tried to buy New Orleans before France offered all of Louisiana.

3. Up the Missouri

Open the Up the Missouri bookmark, follow the trail line and campsites upriver, turn off Watersheds and turn on Biomes, and click along the route for the biome's name.

Where to find it on the mapUp the Missouri bookmark; Biomes layer, pop-up first line (also in the legend): Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands along the Missouri across the Great Plains. Further upriver in Montana the pop-up changes to Temperate Conifer Forests. The campsite symbols sit on the riverbanks.

Accept answers thatNames the grassland biome; gives a reason for following rivers, such as travel by boat, drinking water, food, or a route through open country without roads or maps.

4. Across the Rockies

Open the Across the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark. Note where the trail leaves the yellow purchase, then measure the straight-line distance from the trail's eastern end at Pittsburgh to its western end on the Pacific coast.

Where to find it on the mapAcross the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark; Territorial acquisitions to 1803 layer with the legend: the trail crosses out of the yellow purchase in the Rocky Mountains (the Continental Divide, on the Montana–Idaho border) and the Pacific Northwest is unshaded, so it was not part of the purchase. Measure tool, Pittsburgh to the trail's end at the mouth of the Columbia River: about 2,200 miles (accept 2,100 to 2,300).

Accept answers thatSays the trail leaves the purchase at the Rockies and the Pacific coast was outside it; a measured distance in the accepted range; may note that the straight line is less than half the trail's 4,900 miles because the Corps followed winding rivers and mountain passes.

NotesThe basemap has no place names: Pittsburgh is where the trail line starts, at the fork where the Ohio River begins; the western end is where the line reaches the ocean.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Accept answers that give the purchase's size and price from the pop-up and use the watersheds, rivers or trail as evidence of what the land offered (rivers to the Gulf, plains, a route west) and why New Orleans and the Mississippi mattered to western farmers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; sketch pins for New Orleans and for two places on the trail, with notes (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them); or a short talk using the map. The question of whose land this was is in Looking back: the map has no Native nations layer, so it is answered from Before you start (the Corps met more than 50 Tribal Nations) and reasoning, not from the map.

A model answer (level 4)

The Louisiana Purchase roughly doubled the United States and gave it the rivers western farmers depended on, and the Mississippi mattered because those rivers all reached the sea through New Orleans. At The Louisiana Purchase bookmark, the legend shows the green land of 1783 and the yellow purchase, and the yellow area is about the same size as the green. The Louisiana Purchase 1803 pop-up Notes say it was 530,000,000 acres, bought from France in 1803 for $15 million. When I turned on United States Watersheds, the two big brown outlines had pop-ups named Ohio Region and Missouri Region, and following those rivers on the basemap, both join the Mississippi, which reaches the Gulf of Mexico at New Orleans. That is why the port mattered: whoever held New Orleans could stop or tax farmers' crops on the way to market. At the Up the Missouri bookmark the Biomes pop-up reads Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands, and the campsite symbols sit on the riverbanks, so the new land was open plains the Corps crossed by river. Measure from Pittsburgh to the trail's end at the mouth of the Columbia River gives about 2,200 miles, less than half the trail's 4,900 miles. One limit is that the trail leaves the yellow purchase at the Rockies, so the Pacific coast was not part of what the United States bought, and the map has no layer for the Native nations who governed most of this land.

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did the War of 1812 and the years after it change the United States' place in North and South America?

1. Where was the war fought?

Open The War of 1812 bookmark and use the battle diamonds to find the three main areas of fighting.

Where to find it on the mapThe War of 1812 bookmark; Battles of the War of 1812 layer. The pop-up gives the battle name and its State Name field; the legend gives the result by color. Three clusters: the Great Lakes and the border with British Canada (pop-ups say Michigan, Ohio, New York, Ontario); Chesapeake Bay (Maryland, Virginia); the Gulf Coast and Alabama (Alabama, Louisiana).

Accept answers thatThree areas named by region or by the states in the pop-ups: the Canadian border and Great Lakes; the Chesapeake Bay area around Washington and Baltimore; the South along the Gulf Coast and in Alabama. Accept the Creek War battles in Alabama as part of the southern area.

NotesAround Chesapeake Bay the British won at Bladensburg and burned Washington, then failed to take Baltimore. The Alabama battles were the Creek War against the Red Stick Creeks. The layer also includes Tippecanoe (November 1811), fought before the war against a Native confederacy; a battle diamond may sit on tan battlefield land, so the pop-up may say 1 of 2.

2. The biggest battles

Click the largest diamonds to find the battles with the most casualties, their dates and results, and compare the date of New Orleans with the Treaty of Ghent.

Where to find it on the mapBattles of the War of 1812 layer, the three largest diamonds: pop-up fields Battle Dates, Battle Victor and Total Casualties, with the state in State Name. Legend: blue = American victory, red = British victory, gray = inconclusive. The table lists the five largest in case students pick a different third.

Accept answers thatThe three battles with the most casualties, each with place, date and result from the pop-up; New Orleans (January 8, 1815) identified as the battle fought after the Treaty of Ghent.

Answer key
BattleDatesResultCasualties
Siege of Fort Erie (Ontario)Dates: August 4 – September 21, 1814Result: American victoryCasualties: 2,628
New Orleans (Louisiana)Dates: January 8, 1815Result: American victoryCasualties: 2,096
Lundy's Lane (Ontario)Dates: July 25, 1814Result: InconclusiveCasualties: 1,731
Horseshoe Bend (Alabama)Dates: March 27, 1814Result: American victory over the Red Stick CreeksCasualties: 1,339
Queenston Heights (Ontario)Dates: October 13, 1812Result: British victoryCasualties: 1,233

NotesFort Erie, New Orleans and Lundy's Lane are the three largest; news of the peace hadn't crossed the Atlantic before New Orleans. Horseshoe Bend (fourth largest) was fought against the Red Stick Creeks, not the British: the legend's British label is the layer's simplification, and the pop-up names Menawa as the opposing leader.

3. Florida and a new border

Open The 1819 boundary bookmark, turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and the Adams–Onís Treaty line, and read their pop-ups to describe what the treaty settled.

Where to find it on the mapThe 1819 boundary bookmark. Land Spain gave up in 1819 layer: green areas East Florida (Spanish Cession) 1819, West Florida (Spanish Cession) 1819 and Spanish Cession 1819; the Notes in each pop-up say the land came through the Adams-Onís Treaty and the United States assumed $5 million in claims instead of paying. Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819 layer, pop-ups part 1 to part 7: the Sabine River north to 32° N; north to the Red River; the Red River west to 100° W; north along 100° W to the Arkansas River; the Arkansas upstream to its source; north to 42° N; west along 42° N to the Pacific.

Accept answers thatFlorida (East and West) gained from Spain, with the $5 million in claims if read; the border described using at least the Sabine, Red and Arkansas rivers, 100° W and 42° N, in order from the Gulf to the Pacific.

NotesThe United States already held much of West Florida. The treaty was signed in 1819 and ratified in 1821. The line is drawn from the treaty's description and is approximate, as each pop-up's note says.

4. New nations and the Monroe Doctrine

Open Latin America in 1825, turn on the independence layer, and compare the dates of independence and US recognition with President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823.

Where to find it on the mapLatin America in 1825 bookmark; Latin American independence and US recognition layer (legend: blue circle = recognized by the United States by 1824, orange diamond = recognized later). Six blue circles; the pop-up's US recognition line gives the date. Before December 2, 1823: Republic of Colombia (June 19, 1822), Mexico (December 12, 1822), Buenos Ayres (January 27, 1823) and Chile (January 27, 1823). Brazil (May 26, 1824) and the Federation of Central America (August 4, 1824) are blue but were recognized after the message.

Accept answers thatThe four nations recognized before the message, read from the pop-up dates (not all six blue circles); a reason for the warning that uses the map, such as new independent nations across the Americas that European powers might try to take back, or the United States wanting to be the main power in the region.

MexicoIndependence: 1821Recognized by the United States: December 12, 1822
Buenos Ayres (Argentina)Independence: 1816Recognized by the United States: January 27, 1823
ChileIndependence: 1818Recognized by the United States: January 27, 1823
BrazilIndependence: 1822Recognized by the United States: May 26, 1824
Federation of Central AmericaIndependence: 1821Recognized by the United States: August 4, 1824

NotesMonroe warned European powers not to set up new colonies in the Americas or interfere with the newly independent nations, and said the United States would stay out of Europe's wars. Haiti, independent since 1804, was not recognized until 1862 (orange diamond).

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; a sketch of the three war fronts and of the 1819 border and the area the Monroe Doctrine covered (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them); or a short talk using the map. Accept answers that use the battles to show the war ended without gains, the 1819 layers to show the United States growing and fixing its border with Spain, and the independence layer to show the new nations the Monroe Doctrine spoke for.

A model answer (level 4)

The War of 1812 did not change the United States' borders, but in the years after it the country fixed its boundary with Spain all the way to the Pacific and spoke for the new nations of Latin America, so by 1823 it was acting as the main power in the Americas. In the Battles of the War of 1812 layer, the biggest diamond is the Siege of Fort Erie in Ontario, with 2,628 casualties in the pop-up, and the legend shows blue American and red British victories on every front, from the Great Lakes to Chesapeake Bay and the Gulf Coast. The New Orleans pop-up gives January 8, 1815, after the Treaty of Ghent was signed on December 24, 1814, so it came after peace and the war ended without gains. At The 1819 boundary bookmark, the Land Spain gave up in 1819 pop-ups show East Florida and West Florida passing to the United States under the Adams-Onís Treaty, and the seven parts of the treaty line run from the Sabine River to 100° W and along 42° N to the Pacific. In the Latin American independence layer, the pop-ups show the United States recognized Mexico on December 12, 1822 and Chile on January 27, 1823, before Monroe's message of December 2, 1823, but Brazil only on May 26, 1824. So by 1823 the country had gone from fighting on its own borders to drawing a border to the Pacific and warning Europe away from the hemisphere, though Haiti, not recognized until 1862, shows the limit.
